name: Park Hill
builtEra: 1890s-1930s streetcar-era homes in South Park Hill, stepping forward to 1940s-1950s houses farther north
commonPipe: Clay tile south of 23rd Avenue with cast iron inside the house; later clay and cast iron in the postwar sections to the north
sewerAuthority: City and County of Denver DOTI Wastewater Management owns the mains; the homeowner owns the service line to the main
local: Park Hill wasn't built all at once. It was built one strip at a time, heading north. Baron von Winckler platted the first piece in 1887 next to City Park. Streetcar service brought the first real houses around the turn of the century, and the heaviest building came in the 1920s and 1930s. Northeast Park Hill filled in after World War II. So the sewer line under a house in Park Hill depends heavily on which side of 23rd Avenue or Martin Luther King Boulevard you live on. In South Park Hill, a 1915 Tudor or foursquare usually has a clay tile lateral with short joints that roots have been working at for a hundred years. Up north, the pipe is younger but not always better: cast iron under the floor, clay or the odd fiber section outside, and joints that shifted as the clay soil dried and wet. The big Montview lots add another wrinkle, because a house set well back from the street needs a long lateral, and every added foot is another joint.
local2: Park Hill's parkway feel comes from its trees. Montview and the side streets are lined with big shade trees, and the tree lawns between the sidewalk and the curb sit right on top of most service lines. Roots don't break sound pipe. They find the weeping joint in a clay line and fill it. Ash trees need extra thought now. The emerald ash borer was confirmed in Denver in 2025, and ash make up about one in six trees citywide. If an ash over your line is coming out, it makes sense to inspect and deal with the pipe around the same time. We have lined 78 feet of terra cotta on a Denver job much like the clay laterals found in South Park Hill, with no trench across the lawn.
permitNote: Denver maintains only the public main. The homeowner owns the service line from the house out to the main, which covers the pipe under Montview or any side street and the tap itself. DOTI's wastewater permit desk handles the repair permit. Opening pavement or concrete in the public right-of-way brings in two more: one for the cut itself and one for occupying the street while the crew works. Lining from a basement cleanout often avoids a street opening, but not always.
signals: Root balls filling clay joints under the tree lawn
Offset clay joints where the line crosses from yard to parkway
Heavy scale in cast iron between the floor drain and the foundation wall
Long runs on deep Montview lots with more than one sag

faqs.q: My Park Hill house is from the 1920s. Is the original clay line still in there?
faqs.a: Often it is, sometimes with a repaired section or two. A camera run from the basement cleanout shows exactly which pieces are original and how the joints look. If the clay is round and holding grade but full of roots, lining is a good fit. If it has sagged or broken apart, it needs bursting or a dig at that spot first.

faqs.q: Will lining work if the line runs under a big parkway tree?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. That is where lining earns its keep. We clear the roots, and the liner seals the joints so they can't grow back in, without cutting the roots that keep the tree standing. What stops lining is a collapsed section or a real belly under the tree. In that case we tell you and talk through a spot repair.

name: Washington Park
builtEra: Mostly brick homes built 1900-1940 after the park opened in 1899, with some 1890s houses in Washington Park West
commonPipe: Vitrified clay tile laterals with cast iron stacks and building drains
sewerAuthority: City and County of Denver DOTI Wastewater Management; the owner is responsible for the private service line
local: Washington Park is where brick houses and clay pipe went in at the same time. The land sat mostly empty until South Denver was annexed in the 1890s and the park was laid out beginning in 1899. After that, the blocks around it filled in quickly. Most of the houses went up between 1900 and 1940, and nearly all of them are brick. Builders of that period ran a cast iron drain through the basement and then switched to clay tile at the foundation for the run to the main. That clay is now 85 to 120 years old. The pipe itself tends to hold up well. The weak spots are the joints, which were sealed with mortar or packing that broke down long ago, and the transition fitting where iron meets clay. On a camera, a Washington Park lateral usually looks the same: clean pipe, then a joint with a tail of roots, then another. Because the clay barrels usually keep their shape, many of these lines can be lined rather than dug.
local2: The bigger change in Wash Park lately is above ground: pop-tops, big additions and full scrape-and-rebuilds on narrow lots. A remodeled house doubles the bathrooms but often keeps the same 4-inch clay line that served a two-bedroom bungalow. When a new house goes up on an old lot, the lateral should be looked at while the site is still open. It's far easier then than after the new landscaping and driveway are in. On streets near the park, big old shade trees crowd the tree lawns, and they send roots toward any line carrying water. Before closing on an older home here, a buyer should get a sewer scope. It costs little next to what it can turn up.
permitNote: The city is responsible only for the public main. The owner's service line is private from the foundation to the tap, even the portion beneath the pavement. Sewer repairs are permitted by DOTI's wastewater staff. When a street or alley has to be opened, the job also needs right-of-way approvals for the excavation and for blocking the lane, all submitted in E-Permits. On scrape-and-rebuild projects, the builder's permit set is the right time to decide whether to keep or replace the old line.
signals: Root tails at nearly every clay joint between the foundation and the curb
A cracked or offset joint where the cast iron building drain meets clay
Mortar joints washed out so bare soil shows through the gap
Old lines carrying far more fixtures after a pop-top or addition

faqs.q: We're scraping a Wash Park bungalow and building new. Can we keep the old sewer line?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but only if a camera says so. An old clay line that is round, on grade and free of breaks can be lined and reused. That saves opening the street and the tree lawn. If it has sags, broken joints or a bad tap at the main, replace it while the lot is still bare. Doing it after landscaping and flatwork costs more and makes a bigger mess.

faqs.q: Why do Washington Park lines keep backing up with roots even after cleaning?
faqs.a: Cleaning cuts the roots at the joint, but the gap in the joint is still there, so the roots grow back. Clay lines from the early 1900s have dozens of those joints. Lining puts one continuous pipe inside the old one and seals every joint at once. That is why it usually ends the cycle of cleaning that a hydro-jet alone can't break.

name: Highland
builtEra: 1870s-1890s Victorians from the old Town of Highlands, 1900s-1920s bungalows westward, and 2000s-2020s LoHi infill
commonPipe: Old clay tile and cast iron, often with patched sections, next to brand-new PVC on infill lots
sewerAuthority: City and County of Denver DOTI Wastewater Management; owners handle their own service lines
local: Northwest Denver was its own town before it was a Denver neighborhood. Highlands incorporated in 1875, became a city in 1885 and voted to join Denver in 1896. By then, blocks on the bluff above the Platte already had houses. In the Potter Highlands historic district alone, about 571 of roughly 700 buildings are counted as contributing. They range from pre-1893 Victorians and foursquares to later Craftsman and Colonial Revival houses. The oldest service lines in the city are in this part of town, and many have been fixed more than once. A camera run through an 1890s Highland lateral often shows a history in layers. There might be original clay, a length of cast iron from a mid-century repair, a newer PVC section from some later dig, and couplings joining pipes that were never quite the same size. Each change of material is a spot where grade slips and roots get in, so these lines need an honest assessment before anyone promises a liner will fix them.
local2: LoHi has a different problem. Many old houses between Speer and 32nd were replaced by townhomes and duplexes, and each new unit brings a new service line tied into a main that may be close to a century old. The new pipe is rarely what fails. The trouble is usually the connection, or an old neighboring lateral that the construction disturbed. Farther west, in West Highland and Sunnyside, the 1900s-1920s bungalows sit on narrow lots with alleys and detached garages, so the path from house to main can pass under a garage slab. The ground also slopes toward the river in places, and on a slope a lateral with little fall can hold standing water. A liner will follow a sag like that instead of fixing it.
permitNote: As in the rest of Denver, the city takes care of the main and the owner owns the service line all the way to it, including the tap. DOTI issues the repair permit, and digging into a street, alley or walk adds separate cut and occupancy approvals from Right-of-Way Services. Houses in Potter Highlands or Highland Park fall under Landmark Preservation review for exterior changes, so plan the restoration of historic walks or walls with care.
signals: Clay, cast iron and PVC spliced together from generations of repairs
Mismatched couplings with offsets at each change in material
Standing water in low-slope runs on lots that fall toward the river
Service connections cracked or disturbed by neighboring infill construction

faqs.q: Can a patched-together Highland sewer line be lined?
faqs.a: It depends on the transitions. Liners handle changes from clay to cast iron well when the pipes line up and the diameters are close. A badly offset coupling, a crushed section or a sag that holds water has to be fixed first with a spot repair, or the whole line should be burst instead. We show you the footage and walk through each transition before choosing a method.

faqs.q: My LoHi townhome is new. Why would I have a sewer problem?
faqs.a: Your own line is probably fine. The trouble tends to be at the connection to an older main, or with shared-line arrangements some infill projects used, or with damage done during nearby construction. A camera inspection from your cleanout shows where the blockage is. That tells you whether it's your pipe, a shared line or the public main, which the city would handle.

name: Congress Park
builtEra: Platted 1887-1888, with most building after 1908: foursquares, bungalows and early apartment buildings
commonPipe: Clay tile service lines with cast iron building drains; larger clay or cast iron lines on older multi-unit buildings
sewerAuthority: City and County of Denver DOTI Wastewater Management; private service lines belong to the property owner
local: Congress Park began as Cemetery Hill. When the old city cemetery was cleared around 1890, part of it became the park that gave the neighborhood its name, and part became what is now Cheesman Park and the Botanic Gardens. The surrounding land was platted into ten subdivisions in 1887 and 1888 and annexed in 1889. Real growth came only after a second water reservoir went in around 1908. That timing matters. Most houses here date from about 1908 into the 1920s: square brick foursquares, bungalows and a scattering of small apartment buildings. Their service lines are clay tile, laid in short lengths with joints that were never truly watertight. After a century, the typical failures are roots at the joints, offsets where the ground settled, and cast iron building drains that have scaled down to a narrow channel. Most of these lines can still be lined once the roots are cleared, as long as the clay has kept its shape and grade.
local2: After 1903, the south end of the old park became a city nursery that grew trees and flowers for parks across Denver. Today the neighborhood still has some of the biggest street trees in town, and their roots follow the clay lines under the tree lawns. The Seventh Avenue Historic District runs along the south end and is the largest in the city, so exterior work there goes through Landmark Preservation review. Trenchless methods help because they leave the hardscape alone. Toward Cheesman Park and Capitol Hill, older apartment buildings and houses split into units carry more flow in pipes sized for one family. Those lines clog faster and need a larger-diameter plan.
permitNote: Denver owns and maintains the main only. The property owner is responsible for the service line and its connection, even where that line runs under the street. The repair permit comes from DOTI. A dig in the public way needs its own excavation permit, paired with a permit to occupy the street during the work. Inside the Seventh Avenue Historic District, talk to Landmark Preservation before a historic walk, wall or other exterior feature is disturbed.
signals: Root intrusion at clay joints under large, old tree lawns
Cast iron building drains narrowed by scale to a fraction of their size
Settled joints near the foundation wall of early brick homes
Grease and heavy flow in lines serving converted multi-unit houses

faqs.q: I'm in the Seventh Avenue Historic District. Does sewer work need landmark approval?
faqs.a: Landmark review covers exterior changes, not pipe buried underground. But a dig that tears out a historic walk, retaining wall or other visible feature is a different matter. Check with Landmark Preservation before you disturb those. Lining or bursting from small access points leaves them in place, which is one reason trenchless methods are a good fit here.

faqs.q: Our Congress Park house was split into units. Is the old sewer line big enough?
faqs.a: Often it is sized for one family and now carries two or three. A camera shows whether it's also scaled, rooted or sagging. A sound but undersized clay line may be worth pipe bursting, which can upsize it in place. Lining would make the inside diameter a bit smaller, which isn't what an overloaded line needs.

name: Harvey Park
builtEra: Late-1940s to 1950s postwar tract homes, annexed 1954, with Harvey Park South built out by about 1960
commonPipe: Cast iron under the house with clay tile, and occasionally bituminous fiber, out to the main
sewerAuthority: City and County of Denver DOTI Wastewater Management; the owner is responsible for the private service line
local: Harvey Park went from ranch land to about 4,000 houses in just a few years. Arthur Harvey bought the former Whiteman ranch in 1948, and Denver annexed the area in 1954. The building boom that followed filled the land between Sheridan and Federal, including about 170 prefabricated Cliff May houses. Harvey Park South was almost entirely built out by 1960. A whole neighborhood built in one burst has sewer lines that age together. Most houses have cast iron from the stack to the foundation and clay tile to the main, and a few from this era have bituminous fiber pipe instead. After roughly seventy years, the cast iron often has a rotted channel along the bottom, the clay has root-filled joints, and any fiber pipe has gone oval or blistered. When one house on a block has these problems, the neighbors' lines are usually close behind.
local2: The ranch-style houses here are simpler to work on than prewar homes in central Denver. Laterals tend to be shorter, the runs are straighter, and many homes have an accessible cleanout. Those are good conditions for trenchless work. On one Denver job, a root-cracked cast iron line under a house about seventy years old was replaced trenchlessly over 55 feet. That is the same age and material found across Harvey Park. The exception is fiber pipe. If a section has flattened or collapsed, lining can't restore it, and it needs to be burst or dug out. With whole blocks the same age, a neighbor's camera findings are a fair preview of your own line, and a reason not to wait for a backup before scheduling an inspection.
permitNote: Denver's responsibility ends at the public main. The service line and its tap, including any section under the street, belong to the homeowner. A DOTI wastewater permit covers the repair. If the crew has to break into the street or sidewalk, Right-of-Way Services must also sign off on the pavement cut and on the traffic setup. Trenchless replacement from the house and one small pit can often keep the job out of the street entirely.
signals: Cast iron with the bottom of the pipe channeled or rotted through
Clay joints with root intrusion under mid-century front lawns
Oval or blistered bituminous fiber sections in some houses of this era
Similar failures showing up house after house along the same block

faqs.q: Could my 1950s Harvey Park house have Orangeburg pipe?
faqs.a: It's possible. Bituminous fiber pipe was used in some houses of this era, though clay was more common here. A camera settles it quickly, because fiber pipe has a distinctive look, and when it fails it goes oval or blisters. Fiber that has already deformed shouldn't be lined. It needs bursting or excavation to get a round, full-size pipe back.

faqs.q: Is trenchless realistic for a Harvey Park ranch?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Short and fairly straight laterals, basement or crawlspace access and a single run to the main suit both lining and bursting. The exceptions are collapsed fiber pipe and a line with a real sag. We point out those spots on the video and explain whether they need a small dig first.

name: University Park
builtEra: Platted in 1886 as the University Park Colony, with homes from the 1890s through the postwar decades
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in older homes; cast iron and clay in the one-story postwar houses
sewerAuthority: City and County of Denver DOTI Wastewater Management; homeowners own their service lines to the main
local: University Park was founded around trees. Rufus Clark gave 150 acres of farmland for the university's move south, on the condition that 1,000 forest trees be planted along the streets and in the parks. The colony was dedicated on Arbor Day in 1886. A 1923 plan later called for an even wider variety of street trees. The result, more than a century later, is a canopy that is part of the neighborhood's identity and a steady source of roots for the clay lines beneath it. The housing is mixed. Early homes around Observatory Park and Buchtel Boulevard date to the 1890s and early 1900s, and many blocks were filled in later with one-story houses. The older lines are clay tile that has been soaking up root growth for a century. The newer ones pair cast iron under the house with clay outside, and both give way at the joints.
local2: In April 2024, City Council approved the University Park Historic District. It is made up of about 19 separate properties rather than a single block of houses, including Observatory Park, Fitzroy Place and the Buchtel Bungalow. For homes in the district, trenchless work keeps the lawns and landscaping intact. Around the neighborhood more broadly, pop-tops and large rebuilds are putting more fixtures on old laterals. We take on institutional and commercial lines too. Elsewhere in Denver, we lined 200 feet of 12-inch drain for a university pool. Pipe of that size and length takes the same care as a house lateral, just more of it. On a residential street here, the job is usually far smaller: one clay run, one cleanout and a liner.
permitNote: The city is responsible for public mains only. Repairing the private service line, even where it passes beneath the street to reach the main, is the owner's job. DOTI permits the sewer work itself, and excavating in the right-of-way calls for a street cut approval plus a separate occupancy approval. Owners of one of the designated University Park district properties should ask Landmark Preservation before altering anything visible outside.
signals: Mature street-tree roots growing through clay joints along the whole run
Scaled or cracked cast iron under one-story mid-century homes
Offset joints where roots have lifted and pushed old clay sections
Old laterals now serving remodeled homes with many more fixtures

faqs.q: Our University Park street has huge old trees. Will the city remove one if its roots are in my sewer?
faqs.a: Don't count on it. Denver's responsibility stops at the public main, and trees in the right-of-way next to private homes are generally not the city's to take care of. The better fix is usually on the pipe side. Lining seals the joints so roots can't get back in, and the tree can stay.

faqs.q: Do you work on larger sewer and drain lines, not just houses?
faqs.a: Yes. Besides residential laterals we line commercial, institutional and municipal lines. In Denver that has included 200 feet of 12-inch pool drain for a university. Larger pipe calls for different liner sizing and setup, but the approach is the same: clean it, put a camera through it, then decide honestly whether lining, bursting or excavation is the right fix.

name: Lakewood
builtEra: 1950s-1970s postwar build-out east of Kipling, 1970s-1990s Green Mountain and south Lakewood
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in postwar homes; Orangeburg in some 1950s-60s lines; PVC in newer areas
sewerAuthority: About 21 providers: the City of Lakewood serves only part of north Lakewood; most homes are in independent sanitation districts
local: Lakewood grew as unincorporated farmland and subdivisions long before it became a city in 1969, and the sewer system still shows it. The city's own provider list names about 21 water and sewer entities, from the city's utility in north Lakewood to districts such as Bancroft-Clover, Green Mountain, Lochmoor, Northwest Lakewood and East Lakewood. Many of them were created to serve a single wave of 1950s and 1960s tract housing, and the homes they serve share the same materials: cast iron under the slab or basement, then clay tile or bituminous fiber out to a main that may run down the street or through a back easement. Those laterals are now past sixty years old. Clay joints separate and invite roots, fiber pipe sags into an oval, and cast iron loses its bottom to decades of corrosion while the top still looks solid. A Lakewood camera inspection often starts with a basic question before anything else: which district's main are we connecting to?
local2: One of the jobs we point to in Lakewood was a 67-foot cast iron line under a 1950s home where the bottom of the pipe had simply rotted away. Instead of trenching through the yard, we lined it with Perma-Liner the same day. That is the right answer when the pipe still holds its shape and grade, and the camera footage should prove it before anyone commits. It is the wrong answer on some south Lakewood and Green Mountain lots, where fill settled after construction and left a belly that holds water; a liner follows the sag, so those runs usually need a spot repair or replacement at the low point first. Big silver maples and cottonwoods along the older streets near Belmar and Eiber are the other constant, pushing root masses through clay joints close to the curb.
permitNote: The City of Lakewood states that property owners maintain the private sewer service line from the building to the main in the street, and the independent districts we checked follow the same model. Your district, not the city, may set rules on repairs at the tap, contractor approval and inspection, so identify the provider with the city's lookup tool first. Digging in a Lakewood street needs a city right-of-way permit, and a trenchless repair that avoids the pavement can keep that part of the job small.
signals: Cast iron with a corroded, open bottom under 1950s basements and slabs
Roots packed into clay joints near the curb under mature silver maples
Oval, flattened fiber pipe in some early postwar yard runs
Standing water in settled sections on newer south Lakewood lots

faqs.q: How do I know which sewer district serves my Lakewood home?
faqs.a: Start with your sewer bill, which comes from the provider, not always the city. Lakewood also publishes a provider list and a neighborhood lookup tool, since about 21 water and sewer entities serve parts of the city. That matters for a repair because each district owns its own main and can set its own requirements for work near the connection. We confirm the district before we quote any work at the tap.

faqs.q: Can a 1950s Lakewood cast iron line be lined, or does it need to come out?
faqs.a: Often it can be lined. If the camera shows the pipe is still round and on grade, a cured-in-place liner can bridge a rotted bottom and small cracks without digging up the yard, as we did on a 67-foot Lakewood line. If the run has a belly, a collapse or a joint that has shifted out of line, lining alone will not fix it, and we will say so.

name: Arvada
builtEra: 1900s-1920s Olde Town, 1950s-1970s postwar build-out, 1990s-2020s west Arvada (Candelas, Leyden Rock)
commonPipe: Clay and cast iron in Olde Town and postwar homes; PVC across west Arvada subdivisions
sewerAuthority: City of Arvada Utilities for most of the city; some areas served by districts such as Clear Creek Valley and Ralston Valley
local: Arvada spells out an unusually firm line on who owns what: the homeowner is responsible for the sewer service line from the house up to and including the connection to the city main. That puts the tap itself, often out in the street, on the owner's side of the ledger. It matters most in the neighborhoods that ring Olde Town and spread north and south along Wadsworth and Ralston Road, where 1950s and 1960s houses still drain through clay tile and cast iron. Those clay joints were never designed to keep out roots for seventy years, and the connection at the main is often where a line has cracked, separated or been patched before. Farther west, homes from the 1990s onward in Westwoods, Candelas and Leyden Rock sit on PVC, where the problems are settlement and grade rather than age. Some pockets of the city are served by Clear Creek Valley, Ralston Valley or other districts, so the first step is confirming whose main you connect to.
local2: The city's wastewater division offers a useful service: it will look at a camera inspection video of your service line and give an independent second opinion on what it shows. We welcome that. On one Arvada job for a builder, a 36-foot cast iron line needed a spot repair and then a Perma-Liner liner all the way to the city main, and a clear video made the case for that scope. Arvada also bans sump pump discharge into the sanitary sewer, and homes that once drained groundwater into the floor drain sometimes show silt and gravel in the lateral that has to be jetted out before any lining. Newer west-side homes rarely need that, but their long runs across graded lots deserve a camera check for low spots before anyone assumes a builder-installed line is sound.
permitNote: Arvada makes the owner responsible for the service line from the home through the connection to the city main. Any street cut needs an Arvada permit, and addresses served by a special district, such as Clear Creek Valley or Ralston Valley, may face that district's own requirements at the tap. Check the city's special districts list before scheduling excavation, since the answer decides who inspects the connection.
signals: Root intrusion at clay joints in 1950s-60s lines around Olde Town
Cracked or previously patched connections right at the city main
Silt and gravel in laterals where sump pumps once drained to the sewer
Minor offsets and low spots in newer PVC on west Arvada fill

faqs.q: Does Arvada own the sewer tap in the street?
faqs.a: No. Arvada states that the homeowner maintains the sanitary service line from the house up to and including the connection to the city's main. If the camera shows a failure at the tap, repairing it is the owner's cost, and street work needs a city permit. Trenchless lining that seals all the way to the main can sometimes avoid cutting the street, depending on the condition of the connection.

faqs.q: Can Arvada review my sewer camera video?
faqs.a: Yes. The city's wastewater division offers to review televised inspection videos of service lines and give an unbiased second opinion. We are happy to hand over our footage for that review. A second set of eyes is a good idea before any major repair, and it keeps the conversation focused on what the pipe actually looks like rather than on a sales pitch. It costs nothing to ask.

name: Wheat Ridge
builtEra: 1940s-1960s postwar ranches on former nursery and farm land, scattered older farmhouses
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in postwar homes; PVC in newer infill
sewerAuthority: Wheat Ridge Sanitation District for much of the city; other areas served by districts such as Northwest Lakewood Sanitation
local: In Wheat Ridge the city does not run the sewer at all. Water and sanitary service come from special districts, and the largest, Wheat Ridge Sanitation District, was founded in 1948 to serve homes going up on what had been nurseries, greenhouses and truck farms. The district maintains mains in both streets and alleys, which means a lot of Wheat Ridge laterals leave the back of the house rather than the front. That changes everything about access: the cleanout may be in a basement at the rear, the run may pass under garages or old sheds, and the tap may be in an alley shared with neighbors. Most homes from that first postwar era drain through cast iron and clay tile, and seventy years of root growth from big yards and old orchard trees has worked into a lot of those joints. Other parts of town, including a strip near Kipling, are served by Northwest Lakewood Sanitation District instead.
local2: Wheat Ridge Sanitation District's rules are specific about repairs. A service line is not district property, work within ten feet of a district connection must be done by a licensed contractor, and the district inspects before the trench is backfilled. The rules also prohibit fold-and-form lining on service lines. That is a different product from the cured-in-place resin liners we install, but we still confirm the method with the district before starting, because it is their connection and their call. Large lots with mature cottonwoods and elms are common here, and after years of roots, a clay line can be too broken or out of round to line; in that case replacement is the straight answer. Bursting new HDPE through the old path, where the district allows it, can still keep the yard and alley mostly intact.
permitNote: Wheat Ridge Sanitation District treats the service line as the owner's property from the building to the public sewer. Repairs near the district connection need a licensed contractor and a district inspection before backfill, at the owner's expense. Alley and street excavation also needs a City of Wheat Ridge right-of-way permit, so a dig at an alley tap can involve two sign-offs. Homes in other districts should confirm that district's rules first.
signals: Root masses in clay joints near alley mains behind the house
Cast iron under slab-on-grade additions with scale and pinholes
Separated joints where old sheds or garages were built over the run
Sags on long back-yard runs across former farm lots

faqs.q: Why does my Wheat Ridge sewer line run out the back of the house?
faqs.a: Wheat Ridge Sanitation District maintains mains in alleys as well as streets, and many postwar homes were plumbed to the alley. That means the tap may be behind your lot, and the run may pass under a garage or shed. Knowing the route before any work is important, and a camera with a locator shows where the line goes and how deep it is before anyone digs.

faqs.q: Does Wheat Ridge Sanitation District allow sewer lining?
faqs.a: The district's published rules specifically prohibit fold-and-form lining on service lines. Cured-in-place pipe lining is a different method, but we confirm the approach with the district before we start, and any work near its connection needs a licensed contractor and an inspection before backfill. If your home is served by a different district, those rules may differ, so we check the address first.

name: Golden
builtEra: 1860s-1920s historic core near downtown, 1950s-1970s mid-century subdivisions, 1990s-2000s edge development
commonPipe: Clay and cast iron in the historic core and mid-century homes; PVC in newer subdivisions
sewerAuthority: City of Golden utility; wastewater is processed at the Molson Coors wastewater treatment plant
local: Golden is one of the few Front Range cities where wastewater does not end up at a regional district plant; the city says its sewage is processed at the Molson Coors wastewater treatment plant. Under the streets, Golden's age is the story. The blocks around downtown and the 12th Street Historic District hold houses from the late 1800s and early 1900s, many rebuilt or added onto several times, with laterals that may be clay, cast iron, or a mix of repairs from different decades. Tracing those lines is part of the job, because a house may have been re-plumbed from the back while an original line still runs out front. Mid-century subdivisions on the mesas and hillsides followed, and the ground beneath them is not easy. Golden sits against the hogback, inside or near the county's Designated Dipping Bedrock Area, where tilted, swelling claystone layers can heave in narrow bands and bend a buried pipe.
local2: Golden also combines river gravel and rock in ways that punish open trenching. Along Clear Creek the ground is cobbly alluvium, and toward the mesas and foothills bedrock sits close to the surface. That makes trenchless work attractive, but the same ground movement that justifies avoiding a trench also creates the one condition lining cannot fix: a line that has been lifted or dropped out of grade. On a heaved run we look for water holding in the camera footage; if it is there, part of the line will need to be rebuilt to proper slope. Older neighborhoods also carry mature cottonwoods near the creek, whose roots follow any leaking joint. And on steep hillside lots above town, a lateral may drop sharply to the street; steep grade is fine for flow, but it makes a clear camera record of every joint more important before choosing a method.
permitNote: The City of Golden operates the local sewer system. Property owners in Colorado cities typically own the lateral from the house to the main, but confirm with Golden's utility where the city's responsibility begins before planning work at the tap. Any excavation in a Golden street or right-of-way needs a city permit, and properties in historic districts may face extra review for surface work such as removing walks or steps. Plan permits before the trench, not after.
signals: Mixed clay, cast iron and old repair sections in historic-core laterals
Grade changes and joint offsets where bedrock heave has moved pipe
Cottonwood roots at leaking joints near Clear Creek
Abandoned original laterals running alongside newer replacement lines from later remodels

faqs.q: Does heaving bedrock in Golden affect sewer lines?
faqs.a: It can. Jefferson County maps a Designated Dipping Bedrock Area along the hogback near Golden, where steeply tilted clay-rich layers swell and form ridges when they get wet. A lateral crossing one can be lifted, bent or pulled apart at joints. On camera that shows up as ponding water or offsets. Lining does not correct grade, so heaved sections are often repaired or replaced first.

faqs.q: Where does Golden's sewage go?
faqs.a: According to the City of Golden, local wastewater is processed at the Molson Coors wastewater treatment plant, and the city has been investing in required upgrades there. For homeowners the practical point is simple: the city runs the collection system, so questions about the main or the tap go to Golden's utility rather than a separate sanitation district.

name: Evergreen
builtEra: 1920s-1940s summer cabins, 1960s-1980s year-round mountain subdivisions, later custom homes
commonPipe: Cast iron and clay in older cabins and core areas; PVC and ABS in later homes; many outlying homes on septic
sewerAuthority: Evergreen Metropolitan District for sewered areas (also operating West Jefferson County Metro and Kittredge districts); many outlying homes use septic under Jefferson County
local: Evergreen is unincorporated, and its sewer system exists because septic failed. The Evergreen Sanitation District was formed in 1948 to replace failing individual systems in the town core, and it later merged into Evergreen Metropolitan District, which now runs treatment plants and pump stations and roughly 300 miles of wastewater pipe, discharging treated water to Bear Creek. Plenty of Evergreen is still off that grid. Homes on large lots up side canyons and ridgelines commonly run on septic systems permitted by Jefferson County, so the first question on any call is whether a line goes to a district main or to a tank. For sewered homes, the ground is the problem. Granite and gneiss sit close to the surface, lines are often laid in rock trenches or shallow cuts along steep grades, and long runs drop from a house perched above the road down to a district main below the road.
local2: That terrain is where trenchless methods pay off most, because every foot of trench might mean breaking rock, tearing up a retaining wall or regrading a driveway on a slope. A cured-in-place liner from an existing cleanout can rehabilitate a cracked line without any of that. It is not a fix for everything. Laterals that froze and split, shallow runs that heaved in winter, and lines that shifted when a slope moved may be out of alignment, and a liner will copy those defects. Ponderosa pine and aspen roots also find joints in older clay, and cabins that sat empty through a winter can hide damage until the first heavy use. For septic properties the job changes: we can camera and clean the building sewer to the tank, but the system itself falls under county septic rules.
permitNote: Evergreen Metropolitan District says homeowners own and maintain the service line between the district's main, usually in the street, and the house. Work at the district connection should be coordinated with the district before anyone digs. Excavation in a county road requires a Jefferson County right-of-way permit, and anything that repairs, replaces or changes a septic tank or leach field needs a Jefferson County Public Health permit.
signals: Cracks and separations in shallow runs laid over or through granite
Sags and offsets where winter frost or slope movement shifted the line
Pine and aspen roots working into older clay joints near cabins
Building sewers to septic tanks with buildup and failed baffles at the inlet

faqs.q: Is my Evergreen home on sewer or septic?
faqs.a: Check your bills. If you pay Evergreen Metropolitan District, or one of the districts it operates such as West Jefferson or Kittredge, you are on a sewer main. If not, the home is almost certainly on a septic system permitted by Jefferson County Public Health. A camera inspection also answers it quickly by following the building sewer to either a street main or a tank.

faqs.q: Why is trenchless repair so common in Evergreen?
faqs.a: Because digging is so hard. Shallow granite, steep lots, retaining walls and long driveways make open excavation slow and disruptive. Lining a sound but cracked line from a cleanout avoids most of that. If the pipe froze, heaved or slid out of line with the slope, though, the section has to be dug and reset to proper grade, and we will tell you that up front.

name: Edgewater
builtEra: 1900s-1950s small bungalows and cottages near Sloan's Lake, with ongoing scrape-and-rebuild infill
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in original homes; Schedule 40 PVC in rebuilt and repaired lines
sewerAuthority: City of Edgewater sewer utility for most of the city; some areas served by East Jefferson County Sanitation District
local: Edgewater is less than a square mile along the west shore of Sloan's Lake, and it has been a town since 1904, so almost every street carries old small-lot housing. Many of the original homes are modest bungalows and postwar cottages with clay tile laterals running a short distance to a main in the street or alley, often with cast iron inside. Short runs are an advantage for trenchless work, but the lots are tight: side yards may be a few feet wide, and detached garages, patios and additions often sit right over the old line. Edgewater's code addresses that directly. Planned permanent structures over a sanitary service line must be inspected by the city, and if the existing line is clay or damaged, it has to be replaced with Schedule 40 PVC. That rule shapes many of the jobs we see here, especially as scrape-and-rebuild projects replace older houses.
local2: The rebuilding boom around Sloan's Lake creates a common sequence, and it usually starts with a permit rather than a backup. A new owner adds a garage, deck or addition, the city requires an inspection of the service line underneath, and the camera shows clay pipe with root intrusion that now has to go. Pipe bursting is often the cleanest way to meet that requirement, pulling fused HDPE through the old path, but whether it satisfies the replacement rule is a question to confirm with the city first; where it doesn't, a short open-cut run to PVC may be simpler. On lines that are staying in service, mature street trees near the lake are the usual culprits, and a hydro-jetting and camera visit can show whether a line is worth lining. Many of these runs are only a few dozen feet long, so the decision often comes down to access and what sits on top of the pipe rather than length.
permitNote: Homeowners own and maintain the sewer line from the house to the connection with the city main or the East Jefferson County Sanitation District main. The City of Edgewater issues sewer permits, except in areas served by East Jefferson, which handles its own. Structures planned over a service line trigger a city inspection, and clay or damaged pipe must then be replaced with Schedule 40 PVC.
signals: Root-packed clay joints on short runs to the street or alley
Old lines running under detached garages, patios and additions
Cast iron under bungalow floors with heavy scale
Mixed pipe where past owners patched sections with newer material

faqs.q: Do I have to replace my clay sewer line to build over it in Edgewater?
faqs.a: The city requires an inspection of the service line when a permanent structure is proposed over it. If the line is clay or damaged, it must be replaced with Schedule 40 PVC. A camera inspection before you finalize plans shows the material and condition, so you know early whether replacement belongs in the project budget and schedule.

faqs.q: Who handles sewer permits in Edgewater?
faqs.a: It depends on who serves your address. The City of Edgewater runs its own sewer utility and issues permits for sewer work, but some properties are served by East Jefferson County Sanitation District, which handles permits in its area. Your utility bill will usually tell you which one applies, and we confirm it before any work.

name: Westminster
builtEra: 1910s-1920s Harris Park town site, 1960s-1980s suburban expansion, 1990s-2000s growth north of 104th
commonPipe: Cast iron and clay tile in older south-side homes; PVC in most subdivisions built after the 1980s
sewerAuthority: City of Westminster Wastewater Collections; about two thirds of the city drains to the Big Dry Creek plant, the south end to Metro Water Recovery
local: Westminster is where All Sewer is based, so these are the streets our crews know best. The city grew outward from the old Harris town site near 72nd Avenue and Bradburn Boulevard, where the original plat was laid out in the 1880s and many houses date from the 1910s onward. Those homes are the ones most likely to have cast iron leaving the basement and clay tile running to the street, and after a century the cast iron tends to thin and scale along the bottom where water has run the longest. Moving north and west, the housing gets younger in rough bands: ranch and split-level neighborhoods from the 1960s and 1970s, then Legacy Ridge and the other golf-course and open-space subdivisions of the 1990s. The city's rule is the same everywhere, though. Westminster maintains the main under the street, and the owner is responsible for the lateral from the house all the way to the point where it joins that main, so a crack under the curb is still the homeowner's pipe.
local2: Westminster also sits on a line most people never notice. Roughly two thirds of the city drains north and east to the city-run Big Dry Creek Wastewater Treatment Facility, while the southern neighborhoods send their flow to Metro Water Recovery. The city is now evaluating the Big Dry Creek interceptor, a trunk line partly installed in the 1970s, with construction expected to start in 2027 along the trail north of 128th Avenue. That work covers public pipe, not private laterals, but it is a reminder of how old much of the underground is here. The city also straddles two counties, with the western neighborhoods in Jefferson County; the sewer rules follow the city, not the county line.
permitNote: Per the city's own guidance, whoever owns the house owns the sewer lateral from the house to the connection with the city main, and the city maintains only the main. If a backup is suspected to be in the main itself, Wastewater Collections is the office to call. Excavation or pipe bursting that reaches into a city street or sidewalk needs a right-of-way permit from the city, which is one reason lining from a cleanout, with no street cut at all, is often the preferred route when the pipe is a candidate for it.
signals: Scaled, thinning cast iron under basements in the Harris Park area homes
Root masses at clay tile joints near the curb in 1960s-1970s neighborhoods
Offset joints and small sags where clay soils have shifted older laterals
Belly or poor slope in some newer PVC lines from settled backfill

faqs.q: Is the pipe under my Westminster driveway mine or the city's?
faqs.a: If it only serves your house, it is almost certainly yours. Westminster places responsibility for the lateral on the owner from the house to the city main, which usually means the pipe under the driveway, sidewalk and part of the street. The city maintains the main itself. If you are not sure where your line connects, a camera inspection with a locator will show the route and depth before anyone decides on a repair.

faqs.q: My Westminster home is in the Jefferson County part of the city. Do different rules apply?
faqs.a: Not for the sewer lateral. Westminster runs one wastewater collection system across both counties, so the owner-responsibility rule and the city right-of-way permitting are the same whether you live near Standley Lake or near Federal Boulevard. What differs is where the flow ends up: most of the city drains to Big Dry Creek, and the south end drains to Metro Water Recovery. Neither changes what you are responsible for.

name: Thornton
builtEra: 1953-1960s Hoffman-era planned community, 1970s-1990s build-out, 2000s-present growth north toward 168th
commonPipe: Clay tile with cast iron at the house in original Thornton; PVC in newer northern subdivisions
sewerAuthority: City of Thornton wastewater collection system, with treatment at Metro Water Recovery
local: Thornton started as one developer's idea. In 1953 Sam Hoffman bought farmland along Washington Street and built what is described as the first fully planned community in Adams County, and by the end of 1955 there were more than 1,200 homes. The city incorporated the next year. Houses built that fast, in that decade, tended to use the same materials from one lot to the next, so the laterals in original Thornton south of 104th are now roughly seventy years old and typically clay tile, often with cast iron just outside the foundation. Clay itself lasts; the joints are the weak point. Mortar and early gasketed joints let fine roots in, the roots swell, and eventually a joint cracks or shifts. Where the soil has also moved, a joint can drop and leave a lip that catches paper. Those are the lines we see most often here, and many are still good candidates for trenchless replacement or lining if the grade is intact.
local2: Mature shade trees are part of what makes the older blocks pleasant, and they are also what makes digging a lateral expensive. On one Thornton job, 48 feet of cast iron ran between established trees the owners did not want to lose, so our crew replaced it by pipe bursting, pulling new fused HDPE through the old line from two small pits instead of trenching past the roots. Newer Thornton, north of 120th and out toward Heritage Todd Creek, is a different story: PVC laterals built to modern city standards, which call for cleanouts on service runs longer than 100 feet. Those lines rarely need lining; when they fail it is usually a sag or a bad connection.
permitNote: Thornton's wastewater division maintains the city's roughly 511 miles of collection infrastructure and televises mains for roots and breaks. The city's published pages do not spell out exactly where private responsibility ends, so confirm with Thornton wastewater lines maintenance before assuming the city will cover any part of the lateral; in most Front Range cities the owner's pipe runs to the main. Work in the street requires city right-of-way approval, and the city standards govern how new service connections are made to existing mains.
signals: Root intrusion at nearly every clay joint in 1950s original-Thornton laterals
Cracked or displaced joints near the cast iron-to-clay transition outside the foundation
Heavy scale in the cast iron section under slabs and basements
Sags in long northern-Thornton PVC runs where trench backfill settled

faqs.q: Can a Thornton sewer line be replaced without cutting down or damaging a big tree?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Pipe bursting and lining both work through the existing pipe, so the only excavation is at the ends. We did exactly that on a Thornton home where 48 feet of cast iron ran between mature trees. Trenchless is not automatic, though: if roots have crushed the pipe or the line has lost its grade, a camera will show it, and we will tell you plainly that a conventional repair is the better fix.

faqs.q: Does Thornton treat its own sewage?
faqs.a: No. The city runs a large collection system of its own, around 511 miles of infrastructure plus lift stations, but treatment is handled by Metro Water Recovery. For a homeowner, the practical contact is Thornton's wastewater lines maintenance division, which responds to problems in the city mains. Anything on the private side of the connection is handled by a contractor the owner hires.

name: Northglenn
builtEra: 1959-1960s Perl-Mack master-planned build-out, 1970s-1980s infill, recent redevelopment such as Karl's Farm
commonPipe: Clay tile laterals, some bituminous fiber, cast iron under the house in original tracts; PVC in newer infill
sewerAuthority: City of Northglenn, which maintains about 120 miles of mains and its own treatment plant in Weld County
local: Northglenn was planned from scratch. Perl-Mack drew up a 280-acre subdivision in 1959, opened model homes at I-25 and 104th that summer, and by October 1962 there were about 3,000 houses. Life magazine and the home builders' association called it the most perfectly planned community in the country. For sewer lines, that pace means block after block of laterals installed within a few years of each other, using the materials of the day: clay tile to the main, cast iron under the house, and in some homes of that period bituminous fiber pipe. They are all reaching the same age at once. Clay joints let roots in; fiber pipe slowly deforms from round to oval until it blocks; the cast iron under slabs scales. Because so many homes share a pattern, a problem one neighbor finds is often a preview of what is under the house next door.
local2: Northglenn is unusual in running its whole sewer chain itself. The city maintains roughly 120 miles of mains and ten pump stations, and it sends flow nine miles north to its own wastewater treatment plant in Weld County, which discharges to Big Dry Creek or the Bull Canal for irrigation. City crews jet the mains on a cycle of at least every three years, more often in trouble spots. That program keeps the public pipe clear, but it stops at the tap. Fiber pipe that has already flattened cannot be lined reliably, since the liner needs a round host pipe to cure against, so those sections are usually burst or replaced instead.
permitNote: Northglenn states directly that the service lateral, from the house to where it taps into the city main, is the homeowner's responsibility, and it suggests hiring a plumber to televise the line when problems start. The city handles the main. Any excavation in a Northglenn street or sidewalk to reach the tap needs city right-of-way approval, which is worth factoring in when comparing a dig against a trenchless repair from the property side.
signals: Bituminous fiber pipe gone oval or blistered in some early Perl-Mack era homes
Fine root hair at clay joints running under the front lawn
Standing water in low spots where soil movement has left a shallow belly
Cast iron with heavy tuberculation beneath slab-on-grade additions

faqs.q: What does it mean if a camera finds Orangeburg pipe under my Northglenn house?
faqs.a: Orangeburg is a tar-impregnated fiber pipe used in some homes of the late 1950s and 1960s. Over decades it softens and squeezes out of round, and roots push through it easily. If the pipe is still mostly round, bursting can replace it with new HDPE through the same path. Once it has flattened or collapsed, lining is not the right answer, and a partial or full replacement is. The camera footage makes that call clear.

faqs.q: Northglenn flushes the sewer mains. Does that clean my line too?
faqs.a: No. The city's jetting program covers the public mains, on a cycle of at least every three years, but it does not reach up your lateral. Your line from the house to the tap is yours to maintain. If backups repeat after a drain cleaning, the next step is a camera inspection to see whether roots, a broken joint or a sag is behind it, rather than cleaning again and again.

name: Commerce City
builtEra: 1940s-1960s homes in Derby and Adams City, industrial corridor from the 1930s on, 2000s-present northern subdivisions
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in the older south end; PVC in Reunion and other northern subdivisions
sewerAuthority: South Adams County Water and Sanitation District, not the city, runs the sewer mains and treatment for most of Commerce City
local: In Commerce City the sewer bill does not come from City Hall. The South Adams County Water and Sanitation District runs more than 300 miles of mains, 8 to 30 inches across, over a 65-square-mile area that covers the city and surrounding unincorporated land, and it treats the flow at its own Williams Monaco plant in Henderson. The housing stock splits sharply. The south end, around Derby and old Adams City, dates from the town's incorporation in 1952 and the decades before and after, with clay laterals and cast iron that are now well into their second half-century. North of 104th, Reunion, Fronterra Village and Buffalo Run are 2000s-era PVC. The older lines are where we see root-choked joints and broken bells; the newer ones more often show settled backfill or connection problems. Knowing which half of the city a property sits in tells us a lot before the camera even goes in.
local2: Commerce City was industrial long before it was suburban, with a refinery from 1930 and the Rocky Mountain Arsenal next door from 1942, and much of the sewer work here is commercial: shops, yards and processing buildings with long service runs and heavy use. The district keeps both an industrial pretreatment program and a grease-control effort aimed at food businesses, because congealed cooking fat is one of the main reasons its mains plug up. On the private side, grease-coated laterals from restaurants and food businesses need thorough jetting before anyone can judge the pipe, and lining is only considered after the camera shows clean, sound walls. Large-diameter lining for storm or process drains on industrial sites is also an option.
permitNote: The district maintains the public mains and says outright that property owners can have problems within their own private sewer lines, which puts the lateral on the owner. Where exactly the district's responsibility ends at the main is a question to confirm with South Adams County Water and Sanitation before work starts. Work in a public street in Commerce City also needs the appropriate right-of-way approval, and commercial connections may fall under the district's pretreatment rules.
signals: Grease buildup coating the walls of restaurant and commercial laterals
Root-filled clay joints under older lots in the Derby area
Broken bells and missing pipe sections in long-neglected commercial runs
Settled connections at the cleanout in newer northern PVC lines

faqs.q: Who do I call about the sewer in Commerce City, the city or the district?
faqs.a: For most addresses, the South Adams County Water and Sanitation District. It owns and maintains the sewer mains and treatment plant serving the city and nearby unincorporated land. If a backup is coming from the main, the district handles it. If the problem is in your private line between the building and the main, that is on the owner, and a camera inspection is the quickest way to tell which side it is.

faqs.q: Can a commercial lateral full of grease be lined?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but only after it is fully cleaned. Grease hides cracks and offsets, so we hydro-jet the line first and then run a camera to see the actual pipe wall. If the pipe is round and holds its grade, a CIPP liner can bond and give a smooth interior. If there are collapsed sections or long bellies where grease will keep collecting, lining is the wrong fix and replacing those sections is.

name: Brighton
builtEra: 1880s-1920s original town near downtown, mid-century infill, 2000s-present metro-district subdivisions
commonPipe: Cast iron and clay near downtown; PVC across Bromley Park, Brighton Crossing and other newer areas
sewerAuthority: City of Brighton Utilities maintains the mains; flow west of Tower Road goes to Metro Water Recovery's Northern Treatment Plant, east of it to Lochbuie
local: Brighton puts the line of responsibility in an unusual spot, and states it plainly: the owner is responsible not just for the pipe from the house to the main but for the wye, the fitting where the lateral joins the city main. Any backup or clog anywhere between the main and the house is the owner's to fix. That matters most in the oldest part of town. Brighton was a railroad depot in the 1870s, incorporated in 1887 and became the county seat in 1901, and the blocks around downtown still have homes from that era and the decades after. Laterals there may be cast iron or clay, and the connection at the main is often the oldest piece of the whole run. A broken wye under the street means an owner's repair under the pavement, which is where a trenchless approach can save the most digging.
local2: Most of Brighton's recent growth is a different world. The city counts about 40 metropolitan districts across roughly a third of its land, grouped into developments such as Bromley Park, Brighton Crossing and Prairie Center, and those districts have financed streets, parks and water and sewer improvements. Homes there are on PVC, and when something goes wrong it is usually a sag from settled trench backfill or a poor joint at the cleanout. Lining does not fix a sag, since the liner follows the low spot, so those repairs are usually a short excavation. Where your flow goes also depends on location: west of Tower Road to Metro's Northern Treatment Plant, east of it to Lochbuie.
permitNote: The City of Brighton maintains the sewer mains, while the property owner is responsible for the wye connection at the main and the entire service line from the main to the home, per the city's sewer backup guidance. Repairs that reach the main typically mean working in the street, which requires city permitting, and new or replaced connections are built to the city's sanitary sewer standards. In metro-district subdivisions it is still worth confirming with the city who maintains the main on your street.
signals: Cracked or root-packed wye fittings at the main under older downtown streets
Thinning cast iron and rough joints in houses built before World War II
Belly sections in newer PVC laterals from trench backfill that settled
Offsets at the cleanout riser where yard soil has moved

faqs.q: Brighton says I own the wye. What does that mean in practice?
faqs.a: The wye is the fitting where your lateral joins the city main, usually under the street. Because Brighton places it on the owner, a cracked or root-filled wye is your repair even though it sits in the public right-of-way. That typically means a street permit if the connection must be dug up. Depending on the pipe, the lateral can sometimes be lined or burst from the property side to limit the work in the street.

faqs.q: Is lining a good option for a newer Brighton home?
faqs.a: Usually it is not needed. Newer homes in Brighton's metro-district subdivisions have PVC laterals, which do not corrode or let roots in easily. When they fail, the cause is typically a sag or a separated joint, and a liner cannot correct a sag. A camera inspection will show whether a short spot repair is the right fix, which it often is.

name: Federal Heights
builtEra: 1950s-1960s ranch subdivisions, 1980 Northborough Heights, plus manufactured-home parks and apartments
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in 1950s-1960s houses; privately owned systems in manufactured-home parks
sewerAuthority: City of Federal Heights Public Works maintains about 18 miles of sewer; mobile home park lines are private
local: Federal Heights packs a lot into under two square miles. The city, incorporated in 1940 and named for Federal Boulevard, has a little over 5,500 housing units, and its public works department maintains about 18 miles of sewer. What makes it different from its neighbors is how much of that housing sits in manufactured-home parks, where the streets and utilities are private. In those parks the city does not own the sewer lines, and residents are directed to the park office. For site-built homes the picture is more familiar: Homestead Heights went up in the 1950s, Monticello in the 1960s with around 575 homes, and Northborough Heights around 1980. The first two are prime territory for clay laterals with root-prone joints and cast iron under the house, while the 1980 homes are more likely to have plastic lines. Small as the city is, a single street can hold all three situations.
local2: Our work in Federal Heights ranges from single ranch homes to park owners and property managers dealing with shared private lines. A park main that serves dozens of homes behaves more like a small municipal system than a house lateral: long runs, many connections, and a single blockage that affects several families. Camera inspection comes first to map the pipe and its junctions; after that, cleaning, spot repairs or lining can be planned section by section. Public works also targets kitchen grease with an FOG effort of its own, and that same grease is a common culprit in apartment and condominium lines, where several kitchens feed one pipe. Those buildings often do best with scheduled jetting and a camera check afterward, so small problems are caught before a whole building backs up.
permitNote: The Federal Heights public works department maintains the public sewer, and its guidance puts service lines on private property owners. Inside mobile home parks, streets and utilities are private, so repairs go through park management rather than the city. Work that extends into a city street to reach a public main requires city approval, and sewer overflows in the public system are reported to public works.
signals: Root-choked clay joints under 1950s Homestead Heights front yards
Grease-lined shared lines serving apartment and condominium buildings
Cracked or separated joints in private manufactured-home park mains
Cast iron with scale and pinholes beneath 1960s slab and crawlspace homes

faqs.q: I live in a Federal Heights mobile home park. Who fixes the sewer?
faqs.a: In Federal Heights, streets and utilities inside mobile home parks are private, so the city does not maintain those sewer lines. Park management is the first call. Park owners sometimes bring us in to camera the shared lines, find the problem section and repair it, and in many cases a damaged run can be lined or spot-repaired without tearing up the park's streets.

faqs.q: My Federal Heights ranch house was built in the 1950s. Should I have the sewer checked?
faqs.a: If the house still has its original lateral, it is likely around seventy years old and made of clay tile with cast iron near the foundation. A camera inspection is a reasonable step before buying, after repeated slow drains, or before remodeling a bathroom. It shows whether roots, cracked joints or sags are present and whether the pipe is sound enough to line or needs to be replaced.

name: Aurora
builtEra: Early 1900s Original Aurora near Colfax, 1950s-1960s postwar tracts like Hoffman Heights, then decades of growth south and east
commonPipe: Cast iron and clay tile in the older north and central neighborhoods; PVC in most newer subdivisions to the south and east
sewerAuthority: Aurora Water operates the city's wastewater collection system; a few edge areas are served by special districts, so confirm on your bill
local: Aurora's city code leaves little doubt about the sewer lateral: the owner of a connected building keeps ownership of the service line and is responsible for maintaining and repairing all of it, out to where it taps the public main. The code also lets Aurora Water set a deadline for repairs, and in serious cases the city can shut off water service to a property whose failing line threatens the public system, while monthly charges keep running. That puts real weight on getting the diagnosis right. In the older parts of north Aurora, a camera usually shows cast iron under the house turning into clay tile somewhere past the foundation, and it is that transition, plus the clay joints beyond it, where roots and soil movement do most of their damage. Farther south and east, the pipe is newer PVC, and trouble there tends to come from settled trenches, construction debris or a poorly glued fitting rather than old age.
local2: Hoffman Heights tells a lot of Aurora's story. Builder Sam Hoffman planned about 1,700 single-story brick ranches there in the early 1950s, priced for returning veterans and the workers at Lowry, Fitzsimons and Buckley. Seventy-some years later, the sewer lines under those ranches are reaching the age when cast iron scales and thins and clay tile joints let go. Because so many homes share the same builder and layout, the failure points repeat from street to street: the elbow under the slab, the transition to clay, and the joint nearest the main. Aurora also spans Arapahoe, Adams and Douglas counties across nearly a thousand feet of elevation, so a long lateral in a hilly east side subdivision can behave very differently from a flat lot near Colfax. Where a line has lost grade and holds water, we will say so and recommend replacing that section rather than lining over the sag.
permitNote: Under the Aurora City Code, the property owner carries the whole service line. Permits come in two pieces: the building division covers the portion within five feet of the building, and the public works side covers the rest. Any new connection to the public sewer is made under the supervision of an Aurora Water representative, and you must notify the city when the work is ready for inspection. Digging in a city street or sidewalk also requires separate approval to work in the right-of-way. The city may repair a line in the right-of-way at its own expense to protect the system, but only at its discretion.
signals: Cast iron with heavy scale and a thinning bottom under 1950s slab-on-grade ranches
Root masses at the first clay tile joint just outside the foundation wall
Offset clay joints where expansive soil has shifted the pipe over decades
Low spots and standing water in longer laterals on sloped east side lots

faqs.q: Does Aurora Water fix the sewer line under the street in front of my house?
faqs.a: Generally no. Aurora's code says the owner of a connected building keeps ownership of, and upkeep on, the service line all the way to the public sewer tap, which includes the stretch under the street. The city reserves the option to repair a line in the right-of-way itself if that is needed to protect the public system, but homeowners should plan on that section being their responsibility and budget for a camera inspection of the full length.

faqs.q: Can a 1950s Hoffman Heights sewer line be lined, or does it need to be dug up?
faqs.a: Often it can be lined. A cast iron or clay lateral that is cracked, rooted or scaled but keeps its round profile and steady fall is a good candidate for CIPP, which puts a new pipe inside the old one without trenching the yard. If the camera shows a collapsed section, a belly that holds water, or joints that have pulled far apart, lining would only copy those defects, and bursting or a conventional repair is the honest answer.

name: Centennial
builtEra: Mostly 1960s-1990s suburban subdivisions, incorporated as a city in 2001 from existing unincorporated neighborhoods
commonPipe: Clay tile and some cast iron in the western and older neighborhoods; PVC in later subdivisions farther east
sewerAuthority: No city sewer utility; service comes from special districts including South Arapahoe Sanitation, Southgate, South Englewood No. 1, ACWWA, East Cherry Creek Valley, Castlewood and Havana
local: Centennial became a city in 2001, but its sewers were in the ground long before that, laid by the special districts that served the unincorporated suburbs. The city never took them over. Its own district map shows seven separate sanitation providers inside city limits: South Arapahoe Sanitation District, Southgate, South Englewood Sanitation District No. 1, the Arapahoe County Water and Wastewater Authority, East Cherry Creek Valley, Castlewood and Havana. Two houses on opposite sides of an arterial can answer to different boards with different notice rules. South Arapahoe, formed in 1957 and covering the stretch between Broadway and Holly south of Orchard Road, is blunt about ownership: the line from the building up to and including the tap on the district main belongs to the owner. The district also reports that about two-thirds of its own mains are clay or concrete, which matches what we tend to see in the private laterals connected to them.
local2: One Centennial job shows why the approach matters. A homeowner had 47 feet of cast iron that was flaking apart from the inside. Instead of opening the yard and landscaping, we lined it through a cleanout inside the house, leaving a new jointless pipe within the old one. That works when the host pipe still has its shape and fall. South Arapahoe's own guidance on rehabilitation makes the same point we do: lining is reasonable when the damaged line has no sags and its breaks or separated joints are not too severe, and the district asks to be notified at least 48 hours before the work. In the western neighborhoods near Southglenn, mature trees and expansive clay are the usual culprits. Farther east, in newer tracts, the problem is more often a settled trench or a bad fitting.
permitNote: Start by identifying your district, since Centennial itself does not run the sewer. In South Arapahoe Sanitation District, homeowners are on the hook for everything from the building through the tap itself, and the district's engineer must be notified at least 48 hours before a line is rehabilitated. Other districts in the city set their own tap, inspection and notification requirements, so check with yours. Digging in a public street or sidewalk also needs City of Centennial approval through its right-of-way process.
signals: Clay tile joints packed with fine roots under older western subdivisions
Cast iron flaking and scaling inside the foundation of 1960s and 1970s homes
Separated joints near the tap where the lateral meets a deep district main
Sags in longer runs where expansive clay has settled or heaved the pipe

faqs.q: Which sanitation district serves my Centennial home?
faqs.a: It depends on the address. The city's district map shows seven sanitation providers, including South Arapahoe, Southgate, South Englewood No. 1, ACWWA and East Cherry Creek Valley, and the boundaries do not follow neighborhood names or ZIP codes. Your sewer bill is the fastest answer; if sewer charges come bundled with water, the provider named on that bill is usually the district that owns the main and sets the connection rules.

faqs.q: Will my Centennial district let me line my sewer instead of replacing it?
faqs.a: In South Arapahoe Sanitation District, yes, with conditions. The district's rehabilitation guidance treats cured-in-place lining as an option when the line has no sags and the breaks are not too severe, and it wants 48 hours' notice before the work. We follow the same test. If the camera shows a belly or a collapsed section, the better plan is bursting or excavating that stretch instead of lining over it.

name: Englewood
builtEra: Early 1900s streetcar-era blocks, then a 1950s boom that left the city mostly built out by 1960, including the 1949-1957 Arapahoe Acres
commonPipe: Cast iron and clay tile in pre-war bungalows and cottages; clay tile, cast iron and some Orangeburg in 1950s homes
sewerAuthority: City of Englewood Utilities collects wastewater inside city limits; flow is treated at South Platte Renew, which sits in Englewood
local: Englewood is one of the few places in the south metro where the city itself runs the sanitary sewer inside its limits, through Englewood Utilities, rather than leaving it to a special district. The regional treatment plant, South Platte Renew, is here too, near Santa Fe and Dartmouth, and it takes flow from Englewood, Littleton and a long list of surrounding districts. What sits under Englewood houses reflects how fast the city filled in: incorporated in 1903, it nearly doubled in population during the 1950s and was mostly built by 1960. That means a large share of laterals are clay tile and cast iron that are now 65 to 120 years old. The narrow lots on the older grid keep laterals relatively short, but they often run beneath driveways, detached garages and alley-side trees, and those clay joints give roots and shifting soil an easy way in.
local2: Arapahoe Acres is a special case. Built between 1949 and 1957, mostly to Edward Hawkins' Usonian-style designs, the roughly 90-home neighborhood between Bates and Dartmouth was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1998. Owners there tend to care a great deal about the original landscaping, carports and flatwork, which is exactly what an open-trench sewer replacement tears up. Lining from a cleanout, or bursting between two small pits, usually leaves the property looking untouched. A caution that applies across town: an Englewood mailing address does not always mean the City of Englewood owns the main. The 80110 and 80113 ZIP codes reach into Sheridan, Cherry Hills Village and unincorporated areas served by other districts, so we confirm who the provider is before planning the tie-in.
permitNote: Inside city limits, the public main belongs to Englewood Utilities, while the private service line serving a house is generally the owner's to maintain; ask Englewood Utilities exactly where its responsibility ends on your street before planning work. Plumbing work on the building sewer goes through the city's building division, and any cut into a street, alley or sidewalk needs a right-of-way permit from Englewood Public Works. If your address is outside city limits, a different district's rules apply.
signals: Roots entering clay tile joints near alley trees and detached garages
Cast iron with a scaled or rotted invert under 1950s slab additions
Occasional bituminous fiber pipe that has flattened into an oval
Cracked or offset joints at the transition from cast iron to clay

faqs.q: My address says Englewood. Does the City of Englewood own my sewer main?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The Englewood ZIP codes cover parts of Sheridan, Cherry Hills Village and unincorporated Arapahoe County, where sanitation districts rather than Englewood Utilities own the mains. Check your sewer bill: if it comes from the City of Englewood, you are on the city system. If it comes from a district, that district's rules decide the tap, inspection and notice requirements for any repair.

faqs.q: Can a sewer line in Arapahoe Acres be replaced without disturbing the landscape?
faqs.a: In many cases, yes. If the camera shows the original clay or cast iron still holds its shape and slope, it can be lined from an existing cleanout with no trench across the yard. If a section has collapsed or sagged, pipe bursting needs only a small pit at each end. When the line is too far gone for either, we will explain why and keep the excavation as short as possible.

name: Littleton
builtEra: 1890s-1920s historic downtown and surrounding blocks, then heavy 1950s-1960s growth tied to Denver and the Martin Marietta plant
commonPipe: Cast iron and clay tile near downtown; clay tile with cast iron under the house in most 1950s-1960s neighborhoods
sewerAuthority: Collection is handled by about a dozen sanitation districts (South Arapahoe, South Englewood No. 1, Southwest Metro, Platte Canyon and others), with sewer billed through the city and treated at South Platte Renew
local: Littleton is the county seat, but it does not own a sewer collection system. Mains inside the city belong to independent water and sanitation districts, and the city's own list of districts it bills for runs to twelve names, from South Arapahoe and South Englewood No. 1 to Southwest Metropolitan, Platte Canyon and Valley. What the city does own is half of the treatment plant: Littleton and Englewood jointly own South Platte Renew, which receives all of Littleton's wastewater. For a homeowner this split means the bill may say City of Littleton while the rules about your tap come from a district board. The housing underneath is older than many assume. The original town dates to 1890, and the neighborhoods that surround it grew fast in the 1950s and 1960s, so most laterals are clay tile, often with cast iron inside the house and a lot of accumulated root and soil damage at the joints.
local2: A recent Littleton job is typical. The homeowner had 72 feet of clay tile running from the house to the main, with roots and cracked joints along the way. We lined it from inside the house, so nothing outside had to be dug up. That is a good fit when the clay still has its shape.
