Near the South Platte and along the older creek-side streets, though, we look hard for sags and shifted sections before recommending lining, because liners follow whatever grade the old pipe has. Arapaho Hills, a mid-century modern neighborhood on the National Register, and similar 1950s areas often have long runs under mature trees and original hardscape, which is exactly where lining or bursting saves the most.
permitNote: Because districts own the mains, ownership questions go to your district, not the city. Districts in this area, including South Arapahoe, make the owner answerable for the private line right through the tap connection, and they generally want advance notice before a connection or rehabilitation. The City of Littleton handles plumbing and building permits and requires a permit for any excavation in the public right-of-way. The city's online district map shows which provider serves a given address.
signals: Clay tile laterals with root intrusion at nearly every joint on older lots
Cast iron drain lines under basement floors with heavy scale and pinholes
Sags and offsets on low-lying streets closer to the South Platte River
Old repairs where a short section of PVC was banded into clay

faqs.q: Why does my sewer bill come from the City of Littleton if a district owns the sewer?
faqs.a: Littleton bills sewer service on behalf of several sanitation districts, including South Arapahoe, South Englewood No. 1, Southwest Metropolitan and Platte Canyon. The district still owns the mains and sets the rules for taps and repairs, while the city co-owns the South Platte Renew treatment plant. Use the city's district map to see which district serves your address before arranging any sewer work.

faqs.q: My Littleton home has clay sewer pipe. Should I line it or replace it?
faqs.a: Clay that is cracked or root-infested but still round and sloped toward the main is often an excellent lining candidate; we lined a 72-foot clay line from inside a Littleton house without touching the yard. If the camera finds a belly holding water, a collapsed stretch or joints that have separated badly, lining is the wrong tool and we will recommend bursting or a targeted dig instead.

name: Greenwood Village
builtEra: 1950s-1960s acreage homes after the 1950 incorporation, then 1970s onward office and residential growth around the Denver Tech Center
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron under older acreage homes; PVC and ductile or cast iron in newer homes and commercial buildings
sewerAuthority: Several sanitation districts serve the city, including South Arapahoe, Southgate and South Englewood No. 1, plus a Greenwood Village sewer improvement district listed among South Platte Renew connectors
local: Greenwood Village has two very different sewer landscapes. West of I-25, the city that incorporated in 1950 is mostly large residential lots, many carved out of earlier farms and orchards, with homes set well back from the road. East of the interstate is the Denver Tech Center, the office district whose growth from the 1970s on made the city what it is. On the residential side, the combination of long setbacks and big trees means long laterals, and the older ones are clay tile that has had half a century or more for roots to find every joint. Several districts share the city: South Arapahoe, Southgate and South Englewood No. 1 all list Greenwood Village in their service areas, and South Platte Renew's connector list includes a Greenwood Village sewer general improvement district. Knowing which one serves a property comes before any repair plan.
local2: Commercial work in the Tech Center is its own category. Office buildings, restaurants and hotels there are coming up on 40 to 50 years old, and their building sewers are larger, run under parking structures and landscaped plazas, and cannot be shut down for long. Lining through existing cleanouts can often be scheduled overnight or on a weekend, keeping tenants open. We also clean out grease-heavy restaurant laterals before any lining, since a liner will not bond or cure properly over buildup. On the residential side, the High Line Canal trail passes through Greenwood Village lined with large cottonwoods, and properties near it tend to show heavier root intrusion than the city average.
permitNote: The sanitation district that serves your property owns the main and sets connection and inspection rules; in South Arapahoe's area, private lines, tap included, fall to the property owner. Greenwood Village issues building and plumbing permits and must sign off on any work inside public streets. Where a lateral crosses a private road, HOA common area or easement, the association or easement holder may also need to approve access and restoration. Commercial properties may also need to meet the district's grease and pretreatment requirements. Confirm your district before scheduling work.
signals: Long clay laterals with root masses under mature cottonwoods and ornamental trees
Grease buildup narrowing restaurant and hotel building sewers in the Tech Center
Cracked cast iron under the slabs of 1960s and 1970s acreage homes
Offset joints on long, deep runs where soil has moved over time

faqs.q: Can a Tech Center office building have its sewer lined without closing?
faqs.a: Usually. Lining is done through existing cleanouts or a manhole, with flow bypassed or paused for a limited window, so the work can often be done overnight or over a weekend. We camera and clean the line first, especially where kitchens contribute grease, and confirm the pipe still has its grade. A collapsed or badly sagging section may still need a spot repair before the rest is lined.

faqs.q: Why is my Greenwood Village sewer line so long?
faqs.a: Many homes west of I-25 sit on large lots with deep setbacks, and the district main may run along a road or easement well away from the house. A lateral of 100 feet or more is not unusual. The good news is that length favors trenchless methods: lining or bursting avoids digging a long trench through mature landscaping, driveways and irrigation.

name: Cherry Hills Village
builtEra: Estate homes from before and after the 1945 incorporation, with many teardown rebuilds on older acreage
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron on original estates; PVC on rebuilt homes, often tied into an older clay run near the main
sewerAuthority: Cherry Hills Village Sanitation District serves much of the city, with other areas on Southgate, Cherryvale, South Englewood No. 1 or Englewood
local: Lot size drives almost everything about sewer work in Cherry Hills Village. The city's R-1 zoning requires 2.5 acres per home, and even its smallest residential lots start at 16,000 square feet, so houses sit far back from the street and laterals routinely run well past 100 feet. A long line has more joints, more chances for roots from mature trees, and more room for expansive soil to pull it out of grade. Many estates also have a history of their own. The Cherry Hills Village Sanitation District rules require an old septic tank to be abandoned and plugged when a property connects, which tells you some homes here started on septic and were tied in later, sometimes through clay pipe that was never replaced. Rebuilds are common too, and a new house often ends up draining through new PVC that joins an old clay line somewhere under the lawn.
local2: The city's sewer map is a patchwork. Besides the Cherry Hills Village Sanitation District, which sends its flow to Englewood's treatment facility under a connector agreement, parts of the city are served by Southgate, Cherryvale, South Englewood No. 1 and Englewood Utilities, and a string of small water districts still exists alongside them. On a long lateral, the most expensive mistake is replacing the whole run when only one stretch has failed. We camera the line end to end, locate the problem sections from the surface, and then line, burst or spot-repair only what needs it. Where a run has sagged badly across a low part of the lot, we will tell you plainly that lining will not fix the grade.
permitNote: In the Cherry Hills Village Sanitation District, property owners own and maintain their service lines, and the district states it is not liable for damage arising from a private line. A tap permit is required before any connection, the permit runs with the property, and the district must get at least 24 hours' notice so an inspector can supervise the connection; skip that, and the owner pays to expose it later. Other districts in the city have their own rules. Work in city streets needs a Cherry Hills Village right-of-way permit.
signals: Root intrusion at many joints along laterals well over 100 feet long
New PVC from a rebuilt home joined to original clay pipe near the main
Sags across low areas of large lots where soil has settled or swelled
Remnants of old septic connections or abandoned lines found during inspection

faqs.q: Who is responsible for the sewer line on my Cherry Hills Village property?
faqs.a: If you are in the Cherry Hills Village Sanitation District, you are. District rules say the owner owns and maintains the service line and its fittings, pays for repairs, and bears responsibility for damage the line causes. Parts of the city are served by other districts such as Southgate or Cherryvale, whose rules may differ, so confirm which district bills you before planning a repair.

faqs.q: My sewer lateral is very long. Do I have to replace all of it?
faqs.a: Rarely. On long estate laterals, damage is usually concentrated in a few places: a root-packed joint, an offset near the house, or a sag in a low spot. A full camera survey with locating lets us line or burst the sections that need it and leave sound pipe alone. If the whole run is failing, lining or bursting it still avoids trenching the length of the property.

name: Sheridan
builtEra: Small 1890 town that filled in with modest homes through the mid-20th century, plus later commercial development such as River Point
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in older homes; mixed materials where lines have been partly repaired over the years
sewerAuthority: Sheridan Sanitation District No. 1 and Sheridan Sanitation District No. 2 serve different parts of the city; confirm your district on your bill
local: Sheridan is small, about 2.3 square miles and roughly 6,000 people, but its sewer arrangement is not simple. Two separate special districts, Sheridan Sanitation District No. 1 and Sheridan Sanitation District No. 2, handle collection in different parts of the city, and District No. 1 is one of the connectors whose flow goes to South Platte Renew. The town dates to 1890, when it took its name from General Philip Sheridan, whose Fort Logan sits just to the south, and much of its housing is modest single-family homes on compact lots. The laterals under those homes are mostly vitrified clay, frequently switching from cast iron at the foundation, and many have been patched piecemeal over the decades. When a line has had three or four different repairs, the camera tends to find problems right at the points where one material was banded to another.
local2: Bear Creek runs through Sheridan on its way to the South Platte, and properties in the lower parts of town sit on river and creek deposits rather than the heavier clays found up on the plains. That changes what we look for: joints that have separated as loose soil settled, and sections that have shifted rather than heaved. Sheridan also shares its 80110 ZIP code with Englewood, so an address that reads Englewood may actually be in Sheridan and on one of the Sheridan districts. District No. 1 has carried out replacement of its own sewer pipe, which is a good moment for owners along those streets to check the condition of their laterals, since the public main and the private line are separate responsibilities.
permitNote: Each Sheridan district owns its public mains; District No. 2 states that maintenance and replacement of district lines is the district's job, which leaves the private service line with the property owner. Ask your district where its responsibility ends and what notice or inspection it requires before connection work. The City of Sheridan issues building permits and permits for excavation in its streets. On compact lots the lateral frequently passes under a neighbor's driveway or a shared fence line, so we locate it from the surface and talk through access before any pit is dug.
signals: Patchwork laterals with clay, cast iron and PVC joined by rubber couplings
Separated joints in loose creek and river deposits near Bear Creek
Roots from mature yard trees entering clay joints on compact lots
Cracked cast iron under older homes where the line exits the foundation

faqs.q: Which sewer district serves my Sheridan home?
faqs.a: Sheridan has two, Sheridan Sanitation District No. 1 and No. 2, covering different parts of the city. Your sewer bill names the one that serves you. Because the city shares the 80110 ZIP code with Englewood, some homes with Englewood mailing addresses are actually inside Sheridan, so do not go by the city name on the envelope. If the bill is unclear, the city or either district office can confirm from the property address.

faqs.q: My Sheridan sewer line has been patched several times. Is lining still an option?
faqs.a: Often it is, and lining can be a clean way to turn a patchwork line into one continuous pipe. We check that every transition is aligned closely enough for the liner to pass and that the line still slopes toward the main. If an old repair left a large offset or a sag, that spot may need a small excavation first, and then the rest can be lined.

name: Highlands Ranch
builtEra: 1981 onward master-planned build-out, Northridge first, Backcountry and the southern edge in the 2000s-2010s
commonPipe: PVC laterals almost everywhere; ABS or cast iron only inside the house
sewerAuthority: Highlands Ranch Water (formerly Centennial Water and Sanitation District), which treats sewage at its Marcy Gulch plant
local: Highlands Ranch is unincorporated, so there is no city public works department behind your sewer. The collection system and the Marcy Gulch treatment plant, running since 1984, belong to Highlands Ranch Water, the utility long known as Centennial Water and Sanitation District. The first houses went in near South Broadway in 1981, which means even the oldest laterals in Northridge are plastic and only about 45 years old. Plastic pipe rarely rots, so the question here is usually alignment. The Colorado Geological Survey studied thousands of soil borings in north-central Douglas County, including Highlands Ranch subdivisions, and found swelling claystone in the bedrock and windblown soils that collapse when wetted. Along a single sewer trench you can get both: one section pushed up, another dropped. On camera that shows up as standing water in a sag or a joint that has slipped out of its bell.
local2: Be skeptical of anyone who wants to reline a Highlands Ranch sewer on the first visit. A cured-in-place liner follows the pipe it is installed in, so a belly stays a belly and water still pools where the grade dropped. When the problem is a low spot or a pulled joint, the honest fix is usually a targeted dig at that spot, or re-laying the run on proper grade. Lining earns its place in a narrower set of cases, such as cracked fittings or root entry at a joint where the pipe is still on grade. We also find builder leftovers in original lines, like hardened concrete, gravel and scraps of pipe, and those can often be cut out with a robotic cutter or cleared with a jetter instead of any excavation.
permitNote: Highlands Ranch Water tells residents to call a plumber first when a sewer backs up, because problems on private property are the owner's responsibility; the district handles its mains. Plan on owning your lateral all the way out, and confirm with the district where your line connects and what inspection it wants on a new connection or repair. Streets in Highlands Ranch are county roads, so a cut in the pavement typically requires a Douglas County right-of-way permit. HOA covenants from the community association can also affect landscaping restoration.
signals: Standing water in a belly partway to the main, typical of settled backfill
Offset or separated PVC joints where claystone below the trench heaved
Construction concrete or debris lodged in a line since the house was built
Roots entering at cleanout risers and fittings near mature landscape trees

faqs.q: My Highlands Ranch house is only 30 years old. Why would the sewer already be failing?
faqs.a: Age is not the main factor for plastic pipe. The common failures here are grade and joints: backfill that settled after construction, clay bedrock that swelled and shifted a section, or a fitting damaged during a later project. A camera run with a locator shows exactly where the problem is and how deep, which tells you whether a small dig will solve it.

faqs.q: Can a liner fix a sag in my PVC sewer line?
faqs.a: No. A liner takes the shape of the host pipe, so the low spot remains and waste keeps settling there. Lining is useful for cracks or leaking joints on a line that still has good fall. For a belly, the reliable options are excavating and re-bedding that section or replacing the run at the correct slope, and we will tell you that up front.

name: Castle Rock
builtEra: Small historic core from the 1870s-1920s, then heavy 1990s-2020s subdivision growth
commonPipe: PVC in newer subdivisions; clay or cast iron possible under older homes near downtown
sewerAuthority: Castle Rock Water, the town's utility; treatment at the Plum Creek Water Reclamation Authority
local: Castle Rock is really two sewer towns. Around the historic downtown, the county seat that grew up in the 1870s and the rhyolite-quarry years that followed, some houses are old enough to have clay tile or cast iron running to the street, often with repairs in several materials. Everywhere else, the pipe is plastic and comparatively young; the town's population grew by about half in the 2010s alone, and neighborhoods like Crystal Valley Ranch and The Meadows are still filling in. Castle Rock Water maintains roughly 280 miles of sewer main and 10 lift stations, and all of it drains to a regional treatment plant on Plum Creek run by an independent authority. That split matters for diagnosis. An older downtown lateral may be a candidate for lining or bursting, while a recent tract lateral in trouble has usually shifted, settled or been damaged rather than worn out.
local2: The terrain around Castle Rock is part of the problem in newer areas. Subdivisions climb mesas and ridgelines, so a lot may sit well above or below the street, and the lateral can be long and steep or deep and flat. Claystone and sandy arkose bedrock move differently when wet, and a trench cut through both can end up with a slight dip at the transition. Steep lines have their own habit: water outruns solids, which then pile up at the first fitting or flat stretch. We see recently built homes where the camera finds cement slurry, rock or a crushed section from heavy equipment during construction. Some of those are cleared with cutting heads and jetting; others need a spot repair. We only line when the pipe is on grade and the defect is something a liner actually seals.
permitNote: Castle Rock Water owns the public mains and cleans them on a schedule; upkeep and repair of the private lateral fall to the homeowner. Ask the utility to pin down where its piece starts at your tap and what it wants to see if that connection gets disturbed. Cutting into Town pavement or a sidewalk takes a Town of Castle Rock permit for work in the public way, and the on-lot portion may also need a building or plumbing permit. HOA approval may apply to yard restoration.
signals: Clay joints with root masses under older houses near downtown
Solids stacked at a flat spot below a steep hillside run to the street
Sags where the trench crosses from claystone into sandier bedrock layers
Cement slurry, rock or pipe scraps left in new-construction laterals

faqs.q: Is my Castle Rock sewer line more likely to be clay or plastic?
faqs.a: It depends almost entirely on when the house was built. Homes in and around the historic downtown blocks can still have clay or cast iron, sometimes partly replaced. Anything in the large subdivisions built since the 1990s should be PVC. A camera inspection settles it in a few minutes and also shows whether repairs were spliced in over the years.

faqs.q: My new-build home in Castle Rock backs up. Is that a builder problem?
faqs.a: It can be. We regularly find construction debris, hardened concrete or a damaged section in lines only a few years old. Record the camera footage with the depth and location of the defect before any cleaning, since that documentation is what a builder or warranty conversation needs. Then the right fix can be chosen, which is often a cutter or a small spot repair rather than a full replacement.

name: Parker
builtEra: Incorporated 1981; growth surges in the mid-1990s and mid-2000s, continuing east today
commonPipe: PVC laterals in nearly all subdivisions; older cast iron only in a few pre-1980 homes along the original town
sewerAuthority: Parker Water and Sanitation District for most of town (not the Town of Parker itself); some edges are served by other districts
local: In Parker, the sewer is not a town department. Parker Water and Sanitation District, a separate special district, runs water and wastewater for most of the town, and that surprises new residents who call Town Hall during a backup. Parker incorporated in 1981 with fewer than 300 residents and then boomed twice, in the mid-1990s and again in the mid-2000s, so the housing stock is overwhelmingly subdivision homes with PVC laterals. Those lines were installed fast, often by the thousands, on rolling ground cut into the same claystone and arkose that the Colorado Geological Survey flags as swelling across north-central Douglas County. What we find in Parker sewers is mostly installation and soil related: joints that were never fully seated, sags where fill settled, and occasional cracked tees where a wye meets the main line connection. Clay and cast iron are rare here outside a few older homes near the original town center.
local2: Parker's HOA landscapes are maturing. Street trees and yard plantings put in during the 1990s and 2000s are now big enough for their roots to go looking for water, and while solvent-welded PVC resists them, the transitions do not always hold: cleanout risers, a gasketed fitting, or the spot where a plastic lateral meets an older connection. Early root entry at one joint is a situation where a short sectional liner or point repair can be a good answer, because the rest of the pipe is sound and on grade. It is a poor answer if the camera also shows a belly downstream. We map the whole line, with depth and distance at each defect, before recommending anything, so you are not paying to seal a joint on a pipe whose real problem is fall.
permitNote: Customers inside Parker Water and Sanitation District deal with the district, not the Town, on sewer questions; if your bill comes from a different district, that district's rules apply. Across the Front Range, districts typically leave the private lateral to the homeowner; ask yours where its ownership stops and whether it inspects repairs at the tap. Digging in a Town of Parker street or sidewalk is permitted through the Town, and HOA rules often govern yard restoration.
signals: Joints not fully seated at installation, leaking or snagging paper
Low spots in the run where fill soil settled after the subdivision was graded
Roots at cleanouts and fittings from maturing HOA landscaping
Cracked connection fittings near the main on otherwise sound PVC

faqs.q: Who do I call first about a sewer backup in Parker?
faqs.a: Start with the sewer district on your utility bill. For most of Parker that is Parker Water and Sanitation District, which can tell you whether its main is involved. If the main is flowing, the blockage is in your private line, and that is when a drain cleaning and camera inspection make sense. Calling the Town usually just redirects you to the district.

faqs.q: Our Parker home is on a newer PVC sewer. Would lining ever make sense?
faqs.a: Occasionally. If one joint or fitting is letting roots in and the pipe is otherwise straight and properly sloped, a short liner or point repair can seal it without a trench. If the line has a sag or has shifted, lining is the wrong tool because it keeps the bad grade. The camera footage decides which case you are in.

name: Lone Tree
builtEra: First subdivision in 1982; Heritage Hills, Carriage Club and Centennial Ridge in the 1980s-1990s; RidgeGate from the 2000s on
commonPipe: PVC laterals; commercial buildings may have cast iron or ductile iron building sewers
sewerAuthority: Split by I-25: Southgate Sanitation District west of the highway, Parker Water and Sanitation District east of it, and Northern Douglas County Water and Sanitation District for part of Terra Ridge
local: The first thing to know about a Lone Tree sewer is which side of I-25 it is on. The City of Lone Tree lists Southgate Water and Sanitation Districts for properties west of the interstate and Parker Water and Sanitation District for those to the east, plus Northern Douglas County Water and Sanitation District for some Terra Ridge homes along Indian Wells Drive. Southgate dates to 1961 and serves parts of four cities and unincorporated land, while the east side is newer RidgeGate construction. Lone Tree itself only began with a 1982 subdivision of nine households and incorporated in 1995, then annexed Heritage Hills, Carriage Club and Centennial Ridge in 2001. So the city's residential laterals are PVC from about the 1980s forward. The older western neighborhoods are now reaching the age when settled trenches, root-seeking landscape trees and small joint separations start to show on camera.
local2: Lone Tree carries a large commercial load for a small city: Park Meadows, the office towers along the highway, medical campuses and a string of restaurants near the light rail stations. Commercial building sewers carry grease and higher volume, and grease that hardens in a line with a slight belly builds up quickly. For those properties, scheduled hydro-jetting and camera checks usually do more good than any repair. When a commercial line does need rehabilitation, lining is often attractive because it avoids tearing up parking lots and storefront entries, but only after we confirm the pipe still holds grade and has not collapsed. We apply that same test to the older homes west of I-25, where the first generation of plastic laterals is now around 40 years old and settling or root entry at fittings is starting to appear.
permitNote: Because three districts serve Lone Tree, the rules for tapping, repairing or inspecting a sewer connection depend on your address; Southgate publishes its own sanitary sewer specifications, and Parker Water and Sanitation has its own rules and regulations. Owners normally carry the private lateral, though the handoff point is worth confirming with your district. Pavement or sidewalk cuts inside Lone Tree go through the city's public works permitting, and commercial properties may also face district grease interceptor requirements.
signals: Grease buildup in commercial lines near Park Meadows and the highway corridor
Minor joint separation and roots in 1980s-1990s PVC west of I-25
Sags that trap solids and paper where trench backfill settled over time
Construction debris and slurry left in newer RidgeGate laterals east of I-25

faqs.q: Which sewer district serves my home in Lone Tree?
faqs.a: Generally, Southgate serves addresses west of I-25 and Parker Water and Sanitation serves those east of it, while part of Terra Ridge along Indian Wells Drive is in Northern Douglas County Water and Sanitation District. Your utility bill is the quickest way to confirm. It matters because each district has its own connection standards and inspection process.

faqs.q: Can a restaurant sewer in Lone Tree be relined without closing for days?
faqs.a: Often, yes, provided the camera shows the line is intact and properly sloped. The pipe is jetted clean first, then a liner is installed and cured, which can usually be scheduled around business hours. If the inspection finds a collapsed section or a belly, that section needs excavation, and we will say so before anything is booked.

name: Castle Pines
builtEra: Castle Pines North built out about 1985-2010; The Canyons and Timberline from the 2010s onward
commonPipe: PVC laterals throughout the residential areas
sewerAuthority: Castle Pines North Metropolitan District for most of the city; treatment at the Plum Creek Water Reclamation Authority
local: Castle Pines North Metropolitan District is unusually direct about the line between its pipe and yours: maintenance, repair and replacement of everything from your house out to the district's main in the street are yours alone. The district runs more than seven miles of pipe and seven lift stations, and its flow is treated at the Plum Creek plant, a facility opened in 2005 that also serves Castle Rock and Castle Pines Village. The lift stations reflect the terrain. Castle Pines sits on ridges and draws west of I-25, and plenty of homes are on lots where the lateral drops steeply to the street or runs a long way to reach it. Most of that pipe is PVC from the late 1980s through the 2000s, installed in claystone and sandy bedrock. Grade problems, not deterioration, are what usually bring us out here.
local2: The district recommends backwater valves, and on a hillside lot below the street that advice matters more than usual, because a stoppage in the main can push sewage toward the lowest fixture in the house. On the private side, Castle Pines lines tend to fail in a few recognizable ways: a steep run where solids collect at the first flat fitting, a joint pulled open where a slope has crept, or roots from ponderosa and ornamental plantings entering at a cleanout. For newer construction in The Canyons, we look for construction debris before anything else. When a slope has actually moved and taken the pipe with it, lining is not a fix, since the liner would lock in the shifted alignment. Excavating and re-laying that stretch is the durable repair.
permitNote: Castle Pines North Metropolitan District puts the full private run, building to street main, on the owner; the district maintains the mains in the public right-of-way. Contact the district before any repair touches the connection at the main. Any trench that reaches a City of Castle Pines street needs city sign-off first, and HOA design rules may shape how the yard is put back. Homes outside the district's boundaries are served by a different district, so confirm on your bill.
signals: Solids stacked at the first flat fitting below a steep lateral
Joints pulled apart where a hillside slope has slowly crept downhill
Roots from ponderosa and ornamental plantings entering at cleanout risers and transitions
Debris and slurry in lines from recent construction in newer sections

faqs.q: Does Castle Pines North Metropolitan District fix sewer lines on private property?
faqs.a: No. The district says owners are solely responsible for the sewer line from the house or business to the district main in the street, including repairs and replacement. The district handles the main itself. If you have a backup, the district can confirm the main is flowing, and then the private line needs to be cleaned and inspected by a contractor.

faqs.q: Should I add a backwater valve to my Castle Pines house?
faqs.a: The district recommends them, and they make the most sense for homes with fixtures below the level of the street or the upstream manhole. A backwater valve lets flow leave the house but closes against a surge coming back. It needs occasional cleaning, and it is installed on the private line, so a camera inspection first is useful to pick the right location.

name: Boulder
builtEra: 1880s-1920s Mapleton Hill, Whittier and University Hill; 1950s-1960s Martin Acres and Table Mesa; infill since
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in the historic core; clay in much postwar housing; PVC in newer construction and past repairs
sewerAuthority: City of Boulder Utilities, which runs the collection system and the Boulder Water Resource Recovery Facility
local: Boulder's sewer story runs through its old neighborhoods. Mapleton Hill, Whittier and University Hill were built mostly between the 1880s and the 1920s, and their laterals are clay tile or cast iron that has often been patched, partly replaced or rerouted over a century. The postwar tracts that followed, Martin Acres and then Table Mesa, used clay as well; the city itself says a large share of its public sewer from the 1940s through the 1960s was clay pipe that is now reaching the end of its life. The city is lining and replacing its own mains, including the corroded trunk sewer to the treatment plant. Private laterals do not get that attention unless the owner arranges it, and many are older than the main they drain into. A camera inspection in these neighborhoods typically finds root-packed clay joints, cracked bells or cast iron with a scaled and thinning bottom.
local2: Two things make Boulder digs harder than they look. Near the foothills, shallow sandstone and cobble-filled creek soils slow excavation, and on the Hill and Mapleton the yards are tight, the trees are large and landscaping is often decades old. That pushes the decision toward trenchless methods. We pipe-burst a 75-foot cast iron line in Boulder after another contractor had started digging and abandoned the job, pulling new fused HDPE through the old path instead of opening the rest of the yard. Trees matter too. Boulder confirmed Colorado's first emerald ash borer infestation in 2013, and as stressed ash trees decline or come out, their old roots are still wrapped around aging clay joints. Lining is a good fit for cracked but aligned pipe; a collapsed or sagging line is a bursting or replacement job.
permitNote: The City of Boulder maintains its public mains; the building's service line is generally the property owner's, but confirm with Boulder Utilities exactly where your responsibility ends, particularly at the tap and under the street. Opening a Boulder street, alley or walk needs the city's approval before crews start, and plumbing work may require a building permit. Landmarked properties and historic districts can have review requirements for visible site changes, so check with the city's historic preservation staff if a job disturbs a designated property.
signals: Root-packed clay joints under mature trees on Mapleton Hill and the Hill
Cast iron with a scaled, thinning or split bottom in pre-1930 houses
Offset clay sections in 1950s-1960s tract laterals in Martin Acres and Table Mesa
Mixed materials from past spot repairs spliced into century-old lines

faqs.q: Can a sewer on Mapleton Hill be replaced without destroying the yard?
faqs.a: Usually. If the old clay or cast iron is cracked but still roughly in line, it can be lined from a cleanout. If it is broken or undersized, pipe bursting pulls a new HDPE pipe through the old path from two small pits. Either way, the trees, walks and gardens along the route mostly stay put. A camera inspection tells us which method the pipe will allow.

faqs.q: The city is relining Boulder's sewer mains. Does that cover my lateral?
faqs.a: No. City rehabilitation work covers the public mains. The service line from your house belongs to you, and it may be older than the main it connects to. If your street has had main work, it is a reasonable time to camera your own line, since a new main does not fix roots or cracks on the private side.

name: Longmont
builtEra: 1870s-1920s East Side and West Side historic districts; 1950s-1970s expansion; 1990s-2000s subdivisions like Prospect
commonPipe: Clay and cast iron in the historic districts; clay in many midcentury homes; PVC after the 1970s
sewerAuthority: City of Longmont utilities, which maintains the main sewer lines and runs its own treatment plant
local: Longmont spells out the ownership rule clearly: the sewer service line between the building and the main, whether that main sits in the street, an alley or an easement, is owned and maintained by the property owner. The city handles the mains. That matters in a town with as many alley-served blocks as Longmont's historic core. The East Side district holds 67 houses, most from the nineteenth century, and the West Side district adds 118 more from the early twentieth century, built as the town grew into a sugar beet and farming center after 1903. Laterals under those homes are typically clay tile or cast iron, sometimes running out the back of the lot to a main in the alley rather than the street. Many have been partially repaired with newer pipe over the years, so a single line can contain three materials.
local2: Longmont's crews inspect the public mains, and when they spot roots growing into the main from a private lateral, the city notifies the owner and expects them to have the roots removed before a backup occurs. The city names roots, grease and structural failure as the usual culprits in clogged service lines. The big street trees shading the historic districts supply most of the roots we cut out there. Cutting only buys time if the joint that lets them in stays open, though. On clay that is still in line, a liner seals every joint at once. If the old pipe has sagged or broken, bursting or a conventional replacement is the better call, and we will tell you which one the footage supports.
permitNote: Per the City of Longmont, the property owner owns and maintains the whole service line, including where that main runs in an alley or easement; the city maintains the main and will help determine whether a problem is in the main or the private line. Work in a city street or alley needs a right-of-way permit from Longmont, and replacing the line usually triggers a permit with a city inspection. The city does not provide contractor referrals for private line work.
signals: Root masses at clay joints under mature trees in the historic districts
Laterals running out the back of the lot to alley mains, not the street
Clay, cast iron and plastic spliced together from decades of partial repairs
Grease buildup narrowing the rough interior of older cast iron laterals

faqs.q: The City of Longmont sent me a notice about roots in my sewer. What now?
faqs.a: The city found roots growing from your private service line into its main during an inspection, and it expects the owner to deal with them. Start with root cutting and a camera inspection to see how the joints look. If the pipe is intact, lining can seal the joints so the roots stop coming back; if it is broken, it needs replacement.

faqs.q: My older Longmont home's sewer goes to the alley. Does that change anything?
faqs.a: It changes where we work, not who owns the line. The city says the service line belongs to the owner whether the main is in the street, an alley or an easement. Alley connections are sometimes easier to reach, since there is less pavement, but garages and fences can sit over the route, which is a good reason to consider trenchless options.

name: Louisville
builtEra: 1880s-1940s Old Town mining houses; 1970s-1990s subdivisions; 2022 onward Marshall Fire rebuilds
commonPipe: Clay and cast iron in Old Town; PVC in later subdivisions and rebuilds, often tied to an older existing lateral
sewerAuthority: City of Louisville Public Works, which maintains the sewer mains and runs the city's wastewater treatment plant
local: Louisville grew up over coal. The Welch Mine opened in 1877, the town incorporated in 1882, and at its peak around a dozen mines operated nearby, including the Acme Mine beneath the downtown area. Mining ended by the 1950s and Louisville turned into a suburb, but the old workings are still down there, reported at roughly 50 to 150 feet below parts of town. The Colorado Geological Survey has studied subsidence across the Boulder-Weld coalfield, and one known effect is that settling ground can change the slope of gravity pipes. For an Old Town house with a clay or cast iron lateral from the early 1900s, that is one more reason a line can hold water where it should not. We camera first and measure grade before recommending anything, because a sag caused by ground movement is not something a liner can correct.
local2: The Marshall Fire destroyed more than 550 homes in Louisville in December 2021, with Coal Creek Ranch alone losing about 160. Rebuilding has meant connecting brand-new houses to sewer laterals that survived underground. That is often fine, but those lines went through intense heat near the foundation, demolition by heavy equipment, debris removal and new foundation excavation. We have seen how that sequence can crack a cleanout, crush a shallow section or leave debris inside the pipe. A camera inspection before the new house connects, and before landscaping goes in over the route, is inexpensive insurance. If the old lateral was clay or an older plastic, it may be the right time to replace it while the yard is still open.
permitNote: Louisville's Public Works Operations Division maintains the city's water and sewer mains; what runs under your yard is ordinarily yours, though Public Works can confirm where the city takes over at the connection. Louisville must permit any cut into a city street, and rebuild projects go through the city's building permit process, which is the right point to ask about any sewer connection requirements. Keep camera footage of a reused lateral with your rebuild records.
signals: Clay or cast iron with root intrusion under Old Town mining-era houses
Sags or reversed grade that may reflect settling ground over old mine workings
Cracked cleanouts or crushed shallow sections on Marshall Fire rebuild lots
Construction and demolition debris sitting inside laterals reused on rebuilds

faqs.q: We are rebuilding after the Marshall Fire. Should we reuse our old sewer line?
faqs.a: Possibly, but inspect it first. The pipe was underground during the fire, then crews demolished the house, removed debris and dug a new foundation above it. A camera run shows whether the lateral is intact, clean and on grade. If it is, reuse can be reasonable. If it is cracked, crushed or an older material, replacing it before final grading is far easier than later.

faqs.q: Does old mining under Louisville affect sewer lines?
faqs.a: It can. Parts of town sit over abandoned coal workings, and ground settlement can change a sewer's slope or open joints. Not every Old Town sewer problem is caused by mining, since age and roots are more common, but when the camera shows unexpected sags, measuring the grade helps decide between a spot repair and a full replacement.

name: Lafayette
builtEra: 1888-1920s Old Town coal-camp houses; 1960s-1980s expansion; 1990s-2010s subdivisions
commonPipe: Cast iron and clay in Old Town; clay in midcentury homes; PVC in newer subdivisions
sewerAuthority: City of Lafayette Public Works, which operates the sewer collection system and the city's water reclamation plant
local: Lafayette started as a coal town. Mary Miller filed the town plat in 1888 on land where coal had been found a few years earlier, and the Simpson Mine and others soon ran beneath and around it. By 1914 it was a busy mining town, and many of the small frame houses in Old Town date from those decades, with cast iron or clay laterals running out to the street. Mining left something else behind. Old workings lie roughly 50 to 150 feet down beneath parts of the city, and a sinkhole there has made local news. The Colorado Geological Survey notes that subsidence can break utility lines and leave gravity systems unable to drain. For sewer work, that means we check grade along the full length of an Old Town line rather than assuming a clog is the whole story.
local2: One of our Lafayette jobs shows why trenchless options matter in the older blocks. The home had 44 feet of cast iron that was close to collapse, and replacing it conventionally would have meant tearing out a porch and a driveway. Because the pipe still held its shape and slope, we lined it instead, and the porch and driveway stayed where they were. That is the right outcome only when the host pipe allows it. Had the camera shown a section already collapsed, or a sag from settling ground, the answer would have been excavating that spot or bursting the line. Lafayette's mature street trees, including ash now threatened by emerald ash borer, keep sending roots into the open joints of older clay.
permitNote: The City of Lafayette maintains its public sewer mains and treatment plant; homeowners generally carry their own lateral, with Lafayette Public Works the place to confirm where the city's share begins at the tap. Digging into Lafayette streets or alleys calls for a city permit, and on-lot sewer replacement is normally permitted and inspected under the city's adopted building code. Ask Public Works about tap location before a crew mobilizes.
signals: Cast iron with a rotted or flattened bottom under Old Town houses
Clay joints opened by roots from large, decades-old street trees
Unexpected sags that call for grade checks near old mine areas
Porches, garages and driveways built over the original sewer route

faqs.q: Can an old cast iron sewer in Lafayette's Old Town be lined?
faqs.a: If it still holds its shape and slope, yes. We lined a 44-foot Lafayette cast iron line that was near collapse and saved the porch and driveway built over it. The camera decides: cracks, holes and scaling can be lined, but a fully collapsed section or a belly needs excavation or pipe bursting.

faqs.q: Could coal mining under Lafayette be why my sewer keeps backing up?
faqs.a: It is possible but not the usual cause. Roots, grease and aging pipe account for most backups. In parts of town over old workings, ground settlement can create low spots or separated joints, so we measure grade during the inspection. If the line has dropped, lining is not the fix, and we will recommend a repair that restores the slope.

name: Superior
builtEra: Original Town from the 1896 coal-era plat; Rock Creek Ranch and Sagamore in the 1990s; Downtown Superior and fire rebuilds since
commonPipe: PVC in the 1990s subdivisions and rebuilds; older mixed materials in surviving Original Town homes
sewerAuthority: Town of Superior Public Works and Utilities, which handles water, sewer and storm drainage
local: Superior stayed a tiny coal town for most of the twentieth century, with about 250 residents, then exploded in the 1990s when Rock Creek Ranch and Sagamore were built, reaching more than 9,000 people by 2000. That compressed history shapes its sewers. Almost everything is PVC laid in one decade by production builders, and those lines are now about 30 years old: young for pipe, but old enough for backfill to have settled and for landscape roots to have found the cleanouts. Then the Marshall Fire tore through in December 2021, destroying nearly 400 residential structures in Superior. Sagamore was lost entirely and only a handful of historic homes in Original Town survived. Many lots now have a new house on an old lateral, and the Town handles the mains those laterals feed, along with water and storm drainage, through a single Public Works and Utilities department.
local2: For a Superior rebuild, the sewer that matters most is the one you cannot see. The original PVC lateral stayed in the ground while the house burned, was demolished and hauled away, and a new foundation was dug. Plastic near the foundation can be heat damaged, and shallow sections can be cracked or crushed by excavators and trucks. We also find burned debris and soil washed into open line ends. A camera run before connecting the new plumbing, and a second look before final landscaping, catches problems while they are easy to fix. In the surviving Rock Creek Ranch houses, the typical findings are more ordinary: bellies, loose joints and roots at fittings. Lining seldom fits those; spot repairs usually do.
permitNote: The Town of Superior's Public Works and Utilities department runs the sewer system and publishes design standards for utility construction. Homeowners typically own the lateral; the Town can say where its portion starts and what inspection applies when a connection is replaced or reused on a rebuild. Street and right-of-way digging in Superior is permitted by the Town. Rebuild owners should raise sewer reuse with the Town during building permit review.
signals: Heat-deformed or cracked PVC near the foundation on fire-rebuild lots
Crushed shallow sections from demolition trucks and excavation equipment
Burned debris and soil inside lateral ends left open during rebuilding
Settled bellies and root entry at fittings in 1990s lines

faqs.q: Our Superior home was rebuilt after the Marshall Fire. Was the sewer line replaced?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Many rebuilds reconnected to the existing lateral if it passed whatever check was done at the time. If you are not sure, a camera inspection will show whether the line is original, whether it has heat or crush damage, and whether debris is sitting in it. Checking now is easier than finding out through a backup.

faqs.q: Our Rock Creek Ranch house is from the 1990s. What sewer problems are common?
faqs.a: For plastic lines of that age, we mostly see low spots where the trench settled, joints that have loosened, and roots getting in at cleanouts or fittings near mature landscaping. Most of these call for cleaning plus a targeted repair at one spot rather than lining or full replacement. The camera footage shows how many trouble spots there are and where.

name: Fort Collins
builtEra: 1880s-1920s Old Town and Laurel School area, 1946-1960s postwar ranches, then rapid growth south of Harmony Road
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in the east and west side historic blocks; clay or occasional Orangeburg in postwar ranches; PVC in newer south-side neighborhoods
sewerAuthority: Fort Collins Utilities for most of the city; parts of the south and southeast are served by the South Fort Collins Sanitation District
local: The Laurel School Historic District alone was listed on the National Register with 549 contributing buildings, most of them Victorian and Craftsman homes put up between the 1880s and the 1920s. That block of history, along with the Loomis Addition and other west side streets, is where Fort Collins keeps its oldest private sewer lines. A typical lateral there leaves the house as cast iron, then switches to short sections of vitrified clay tile with mortared bell joints running under the front yard to the alley or street main. After a hundred-plus years, the clay itself is usually still hard, but the joints are not. Mortar crumbles, joints open, and fine roots move in. The Colorado Geological Survey also maps swelling and collapsing soils over the Pierre Shale beneath much of the city, so seasonal wetting and drying slowly pushes those short clay sections out of line. On camera that reads as a pipe that steps up or down at each joint, with roots hanging at the offsets.
local2: Ash trees were a favorite street tree here for decades. When the emerald ash borer was confirmed in north Fort Collins in 2020, the city estimated that ash made up about 15 percent of its trees and a third of its canopy. Big ash, silver maple and cottonwood roots have a long head start on any 1940s or 1950s clay lateral. The postwar ranch streets, like the Circle Drive homes that went on sale in 1946 and the west side infill of 1948, are where we most often find clay that is intact enough to line: roots cut back with a jetter, the joints sealed inside a continuous liner, no trenching under mature trees. Where the camera shows a real belly or a crushed section, we say so and quote a spot dig or a replacement instead of pretending a liner will fix lost grade.
permitNote: The service line from the house to the public main belongs to the property owner. Most of the city is served by Fort Collins Utilities, but the South Fort Collins Sanitation District maintains nearly 250 miles of sewer in its own territory, so check which provider is on your bill before any work. Where the repair ends at the main, and who handles the tap, can differ between the two, so confirm with the provider. Opening pavement in public space, whether street, alley or walk, requires City right-of-way approval first.
signals: Fine root curtains at every mortared clay joint under older east and west side lots
Stepped offsets where swelling shale soil has pushed clay sections out of line
Cast iron under the basement slab with heavy scale narrowing the flow
Sags holding standing water in 1940s-1950s ranch laterals

faqs.q: Can a sewer line under a historic house in Old Town be fixed without digging up the yard?
faqs.a: Usually. Many laterals in the Laurel School and Loomis areas have cracked joints and roots yet keep a round profile, which makes them good candidates for cured-in-place lining from a cleanout. That leaves porches, walks and old trees alone. If the camera shows a crushed section or a bad sag, lining alone will not cure it, and we will recommend digging up just that spot or bursting in new pipe.

faqs.q: Our ash tree was removed for emerald ash borer. Will the roots still cause sewer trouble?
faqs.a: Dead roots stop growing, but any roots already inside the pipe stay there and keep catching paper and grease until they are cut out. Removal can also change how the soil around the lateral holds water. A camera inspection after the tree comes down shows whether jetting is enough or whether the damaged joints should be lined before a new tree is planted nearby.

name: Loveland
builtEra: 1890s-1930s downtown and West Fourth and Fifth Street districts, postwar growth into the 1970s, then large east-side development
commonPipe: Clay tile with cast iron inside the house in the historic core; clay and some fiber pipe in 1950s-1960s homes; PVC east of Boyd Lake and in newer west-side subdivisions
sewerAuthority: City of Loveland Utilities (Loveland Water and Power), which has provided wastewater service since 1902
local: Loveland's municipal sewer service goes back to 1902, only two decades after the town incorporated along the Colorado Central Railroad. The homes that grew up around it are still standing: the West Fifth Street district holds houses from 1891 through 1932, and every home in the 800 and 900 blocks of West Fourth Street was built by one builder, William W. Green, mostly in the 1920s. A block built by one hand tends to share one plumbing method, so when one of those laterals fails the neighbors' usually carry the same weaknesses. Expect a cast iron drain under the house that runs into clay tile somewhere near the foundation, laid in short lengths with packed or mortared joints. Those joints are the weak points. Decades of soil movement and root pressure open them up, and the transition from iron to clay is a common spot for a separation or a broken hub.
local2: The sugar factory ran here from 1901 to 1977, and orchards and farm fields around it gave way to neighborhoods in stages. That leaves Loveland with a mixed picture: 1950s and 1960s tract streets with clay laterals, and miles of newer homes toward Centerra and around the lakes where PVC is the norm and trouble is more often a construction defect than age. Near the Big Thompson, flood deposits of sand and cobble change the digging conditions from one lot to the next. For the older clay, lining from a cleanout avoids tearing out mature landscaping and front walks. For a lateral that has lost its slope, we will tell you a liner will copy that sag rather than correct it, and price the dig.
permitNote: The City of Loveland owns and maintains the public mains and treats wastewater at its own reclamation facility, expanded in 2019. The private service line belongs to the property owner; before planning a repair, ask the utility exactly which piece at the main is yours. If the dig reaches pavement the City controls, a right-of-way permit comes first; building staff can tell you whether the private repair also needs a plumbing permit.
signals: Separated or cracked hubs where cast iron meets clay near the foundation
Roots packed into clay joints under older West Fourth and Fifth Street lots
Construction debris or poorly bedded PVC in some newer east-side laterals
Low spots in 1950s-1960s clay lines that hold wipes and grease

faqs.q: My house is in one of Loveland's historic districts. Does a sewer repair change the look of the property?
faqs.a: It does not have to. Lining or bursting works from a cleanout and a small access pit, so the front yard, trees and walks can stay as they are. Historic designation mainly concerns what you see from the street, but check with the City before any exterior work. If the camera shows a collapsed section, a small, targeted dig is still less disruptive than trenching the whole lawn.

faqs.q: We live in a newer Loveland home. Why is the sewer already backing up?
faqs.a: In homes built in the last twenty or thirty years the pipe is usually PVC, which does not rust or let roots in easily. Early problems more often come from a joint that was not fully seated, a sag where the trench was poorly compacted, or debris left in the line during construction. A camera inspection pinpoints it, and in many cases a spot repair is the honest answer rather than lining the whole run.

name: Berthoud
builtEra: 1880s-1920s Old Town after the 1884 move, modest postwar infill, and mostly post-2000 subdivisions
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in Old Town; PVC in Heron Lakes, Prairie Star and other recent subdivisions
sewerAuthority: Town of Berthoud Wastewater Division, which also runs four lift stations and the town treatment plant
local: Berthoud literally picked itself up and moved. In the winter of 1883-84, residents hauled buildings on wheels about a mile north from the Little Thompson River bottom to the higher ground where downtown sits today, because trains struggled to climb out of the valley. The town incorporated in 1888, and the grid of homes that followed is the only part of Berthoud with truly old sewer lines. Those Old Town houses, many from the 1890s through the 1920s, generally drain through cast iron inside the house and clay tile out to the main. Some of the first sewer connections came decades after the houses themselves, so it is common to find an odd mix of materials and repairs spliced together over the years. On camera, the problems tend to be joints that have opened up, roots from big yard trees, and cast iron whose bottom has worn thin.
local2: Berthoud's population roughly doubled between 2000 and 2020, from about 4,800 to over 10,300 people, and most of that growth happened in newer subdivisions such as Heron Lakes and Prairie Star. Those homes have PVC laterals, and for them the useful service is often a clear camera look rather than a big repair: checking a sag, a bad joint or a line damaged by landscaping or fence posts. In Old Town, the calculation is different. A clay lateral under a century-old lot can often be lined in a day, sealing the joints without removing a mature tree. If the line has settled badly or collapsed, we will recommend excavation or bursting and explain why.
permitNote: The Town of Berthoud's Wastewater Division maintains the town-owned mains, lift stations and treatment plant. The lateral from the house to the main is private, so ask the Town where the owner's share stops and what the Town requires before work on the connection. Excavating in a town street or alley calls for Town right-of-way approval, and a building permit may apply to the plumbing work itself. Berthoud straddles the Larimer-Weld line, yet inside the town's service area one utility handles sewer on both sides of that line.
signals: Patched and mixed pipe materials under Old Town homes from later sewer hookups
Roots at clay joints under large backyard trees on older lots
Worn-through bottoms in cast iron drains beneath older houses
Settled or crushed PVC in newer yards after landscaping or fencing work

faqs.q: Is lining worth it for a small Old Town Berthoud lateral?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many of those laterals are short runs of clay with cracked joints and roots but a sound shape, which is exactly what a cured-in-place liner fixes well. It avoids digging up a mature yard and old walks, and on a short Old Town run the work usually wraps up in a single visit. If the camera shows a collapse or a stretch that has lost its fall, lining will not solve it, and a dig or a burst is the better path.

faqs.q: Our Heron Lakes home is only a few years old. Should we worry about the sewer line?
faqs.a: Newer PVC lines are generally reliable, but they can be cracked by heavy equipment, fence posts or landscaping, and a poorly compacted trench can settle into a sag. If you notice slow drains or gurgling, a camera inspection shows whether anything needs attention before it turns into a backup in a finished basement.

name: Greeley
builtEra: 1870s-1920s Union Colony core and Cranford, 1950s-1970s ranch neighborhoods, west-side growth since the 1980s
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron near downtown and the university; clay with some Orangeburg in postwar homes; PVC on the west side
sewerAuthority: City of Greeley Water and Sewer, which runs about 390 miles of sewer pipe and 11 pumping stations
local: Greeley's sewer system dates to 1889, less than twenty years after the Union Colony settlers laid out their town between the Cache la Poudre and South Platte rivers. The City now maintains about 390 miles of main, and it has used trenchless methods on its own pipe since 1988. What the City does not touch is the private line from each house to that main. In the older blocks, including Cranford, which the City surveyed for its historic character, those private lines are commonly cast iron under the house and clay tile beyond. They were laid when the houses were new, and many have never been replaced. The clay has held up better than the joints between the sections: mortar has broken away, roots have moved in, and settling has shifted some pieces out of line. A camera run through one of these lines usually shows a string of small defects rather than a single break.
local2: Irrigation built Greeley. The colonists had canals watering tens of thousands of acres within two decades, and the tree-lined streets that followed are one reason the old neighborhoods feel the way they do. Those same trees are hard on clay laterals. In the ranch-home areas built in the 1950s and 1960s, like Belair Park and Arlington Heights, we see a lot of clay with root intrusion and the occasional Orangeburg fiber pipe that has flattened into an oval. The fiber pipe is a replacement job; it is too deformed to line properly, and bursting or digging is the honest answer. For clay that still holds its shape, lining gives it a new jointless pipe inside the old one without trenching the lawn.
permitNote: The City of Greeley tells residents plainly that their service line is their own and to hire a private company for problems on it; City crews handle the public mains. Before digging, get the City's answer on exactly where private ownership stops near the main. Breaking into public pavement means pulling a Greeley right-of-way permit, and the repair itself may need its own permit and inspection.
signals: Rows of small cracks and root intrusions along century-old clay laterals near downtown
Flattened or blistered Orangeburg fiber pipe in some 1950s-1960s ranch homes
Heavy scale and thin spots in cast iron under older basements
Offsets at joints where settling ground has shifted clay sections

faqs.q: Does the City of Greeley fix the sewer line in my yard?
faqs.a: No. The City maintains its mains and pumping stations, but the line from your house to the main is yours. The City recommends calling a private sewer company for problems on that line. A camera inspection tells you whether the blockage is in your lateral or in the public main; if it is the main, the City is the one to call.

faqs.q: Our older Greeley home has clay sewer pipe. Should we line it or replace it?
faqs.a: It depends on shape and slope. Tile with root-filled, cracked joints that has kept its roundness and fall is a strong candidate for lining, which avoids trenching mature trees and walks. If sections have collapsed, sagged or turned out to be fiber pipe, lining will not hold up, and the better call is a pipe burst or an open repair of that section.

name: Windsor
builtEra: 1900s-1920s sugar-factory era downtown, scattered postwar homes, and heavy subdivision growth since 2000
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron near Main Street; PVC in Water Valley, Highland Meadows and most newer subdivisions
sewerAuthority: Town of Windsor Public Works, which runs over 150 miles of sewer and the town treatment plant
local: Windsor spans the Weld-Larimer county line, and the town's sewer network now covers more than 150 miles. Most of it is young. Windsor had about 9,900 residents in 2000 and about 32,700 by 2020, and the neighborhoods built for that influx, such as Water Valley and Highland Meadows, were built with PVC laterals. The older lines are concentrated around downtown, where the town grew up after the Great Western sugar factory opened in 1903 and German-Russian families came to work the beet fields. Those early 1900s homes are the ones with clay tile and cast iron laterals, and they behave like their counterparts elsewhere on the Front Range: roots in the joints, scale inside the iron, and cracks where the soil has shifted. Because so much of Windsor is new, a camera inspection often surprises owners in both directions: a 1915 bungalow may have a lateral someone already replaced, while a 2005 home can hide a cracked joint from a careless trench backfill.
local2: The May 2008 tornado cut through Windsor with winds near 165 mph and led to roughly 24,000 insurance claims. Many damaged homes were repaired or rebuilt on their original foundations, and in some cases the lateral under the yard was reused rather than replaced. If you own a rebuilt home near the storm path, it is worth confirming what the sewer line is actually made of and whether it took damage from heavy equipment during cleanup. For older clay near downtown, lining avoids tearing up newly re-established landscaping. For a line that was crushed or knocked off grade, replacement or bursting is the better repair. Town crews are also planning a larger treatment plant as the population keeps climbing, a reminder of how quickly this system has grown.
permitNote: The Town of Windsor asks contractors to notify Public Works before working in the sanitary sewer system, including routine clearing, blockage removal and repairs. The private service line is the owner's to maintain; the Town can say how far that ownership reaches toward the main. Any repair that crosses into the street or walk also needs Town right-of-way approval. Windsor sits in two counties, so Larimer-side homes may use a different mailing ZIP than Weld-side ones, while the Town remains the sewer utility across its service area.
signals: Root intrusion at clay joints under early 1900s homes near Main Street
Mixed original and replacement pipe under homes rebuilt after 2008
Sags and poorly bedded joints in some newer subdivision laterals
Scale buildup in cast iron drains under older foundations

faqs.q: Our Windsor house was rebuilt after the 2008 tornado. Is the sewer line new too?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Some rebuilds reused the original lateral under the yard, and heavy cleanup equipment could have cracked or shifted it. A camera inspection shows what material is down there and its condition. If it is older clay with cracks but good shape, lining may be the answer; if it was crushed or knocked off grade, a dig or burst is the right call.

faqs.q: Do we have to tell the Town of Windsor before a sewer repair?
faqs.a: The Town asks contractors to notify Public Works before work in the sanitary sewer system, including clearing and repairs. We handle that coordination as part of the job, along with any right-of-way permit needed if the work reaches the street or sidewalk. That keeps Town crews informed in case the work affects the connection at the main, and it avoids surprises if a Town crew is already jetting that stretch of main the same week.

name: Erie
builtEra: 1870s-1920s coal-town core in Old Town Erie, small postwar pockets, and mostly post-1995 subdivisions
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in Old Town Erie; PVC in Erie Village, Vista Ridge, Colliers Hill and other newer neighborhoods
sewerAuthority: Town of Erie public works and utilities, which operate the town's sewer collection and treatment
local: Erie was a coal town before it was a suburb. The first official underground mine opened in 1876, and mining went on until the last mine shut in 1978. Much of the Boulder-Weld coal field runs under and around town, and state geologists have looked closely at how old mine workings in this area can settle decades after they close. For sewer lines, that matters because a lateral depends on steady slope. Ground that drops even a little can create a belly where waste sits, or crack a rigid clay joint. The oldest laterals, under the miners' houses in Old Town Erie, are typically clay tile and cast iron. Those lines have also had more than a century of roots and ordinary soil movement working on them. When a camera shows a sag or offset under an older Erie home, it is fair to ask whether the ground itself has moved.
local2: Erie grew from about 6,300 residents in 2000 to just over 30,000 in 2020, and it spans both Weld and Boulder counties, with most residents on the Weld side. The subdivisions that absorbed that growth, such as Vista Ridge and Colliers Hill, have PVC laterals that rarely need lining. When they do have problems, it is usually a bad joint, a crushed section from later construction, or a sag. That is where honesty about methods matters: a liner follows the existing pipe, so if the line has settled out of grade, lining it just seals in the sag. For those cases, we recommend excavation or bursting to reset the slope. For intact older clay in Old Town, lining is often the cleaner fix, sealing every joint along the run without opening the yard.
permitNote: The Town of Erie maintains the public sewer mains; the service line from the building to the main is private. Get the Town's word on where the private portion ends at the connection and what inspection it requires for a repaired or replaced line. Excavation in Town pavement requires a right-of-way permit. Because Erie crosses the Boulder-Weld county line, confirm you are dealing with the Town rather than a neighboring district if your address is near the edge of town.
signals: Sags or offsets that may reflect ground settlement in the old coal field
Root-filled clay joints under early homes in Old Town Erie
Cracked or crushed PVC where later construction crossed newer laterals
Corroded cast iron drains beneath the oldest Erie foundations

faqs.q: Can old coal mines under Erie damage my sewer line?
faqs.a: They can contribute. Where old workings settle, the ground above can shift, and a sewer lateral needs steady slope to drain. A camera inspection with location tracing shows whether a line has a sag or offset. Lining will not fix a belly, so if settlement has changed the grade, we recommend digging or bursting to reset it.

faqs.q: Our Vista Ridge home is on PVC. Why would it need a camera inspection?
faqs.a: PVC resists roots and corrosion, but it can crack under heavy equipment or settle into a low spot if the trench was not well compacted. A camera look before buying or after repeated slow drains shows exactly what is going on, and the fix is often a single spot repair at the damaged joint instead of a whole new line. On a newer home, that is usually all it takes.

name: Frederick
builtEra: 1907-1950s coal-camp core, then mostly post-2000 subdivisions
commonPipe: Clay tile and cast iron in the original town and Evanston; PVC in Wyndham Hill, Silverstone and most newer neighborhoods
sewerAuthority: St. Vrain Sanitation District, the sole sewer provider in Frederick (also serving Firestone and Dacono)
local: Frederick's sewer service comes from the St. Vrain Sanitation District, a special district that also serves Firestone and Dacono plus parts of Mead, Longmont and unincorporated Weld County. The district runs roughly 250 miles of collection pipe and about 15,250 taps. Its policy on private lines leaves little room for doubt: the service line and the service connection belong to the property owner, who is responsible for maintaining and repairing them. That means the owner's share reaches all the way to where the line meets the district main, not just to the property line. In the original town, which began as a coal-mining camp and incorporated in 1907, laterals from the early decades are typically clay tile, sometimes with cast iron under the house. Those older lines, plus the connection at the main, are where most real repair work in Frederick happens. Because the owner's share includes that connection, a failure right at the main is still a private repair here, which surprises many buyers coming from cities that draw the line differently.
local2: Frederick grew from about 2,500 people in 2000 to over 14,500 in 2020, so most homes, in places like Wyndham Hill and Silverstone, have newer PVC laterals. Problems there usually come from a construction defect or later damage rather than age. The older side of town is different. The Frederick mine closed in 1960, and a Colorado Geological Survey study examined ground settlement over abandoned workings in the Frederick-Firestone-Dacono area. If the camera shows a sag in an older line, that history is worth keeping in mind. Lining suits cracked tile whose shape and fall remain intact; it is the wrong repair for a line that has settled, which needs excavation or bursting.
permitNote: St. Vrain Sanitation District states that the owner owns the service line and the service connection, so repairs up to the main are the owner's responsibility. Contact the district before work on the connection to learn its requirements. The Town of Frederick handles right-of-way permits for work in streets and sidewalks. Water service in Frederick comes from the Town east of I-25 and from Left Hand Water District west of it, which matters if a sewer repair runs near a water line.
signals: Cracked clay and root intrusion in original-town laterals from the early 1900s
Worn or separated service connections at the district main
Sags in older lines that may reflect ground settlement over old mines
Bedding or joint defects in some newer PVC laterals

faqs.q: Who pays to fix the sewer connection at the main in Frederick?
faqs.a: Under St. Vrain Sanitation District's rules, the property owner owns the service line and the service connection, so repairs up to the main are the owner's responsibility. The district handles its own mains. Before any work at the connection, contact the district so the repair meets its requirements. A camera inspection shows whether the problem is at the connection or elsewhere in the lateral.

faqs.q: Should an older Frederick sewer line be lined or replaced?
faqs.a: If the clay is cracked but still holds its round shape and slope, lining works well and avoids trenching. If the line has sagged, collapsed or shifted, perhaps from ground settlement in this old mining area, lining will not correct the grade. Then the choice is between bursting a new line into place or digging out the bad stretch.
